metadata.title: What is a VAR (Value-Added Reseller)?
metadata.author: Eye on Tech
metadata.shortDescription:
AWS shifts its business model: https://www.techtarget.com/searchitchannel/news/252510467/AWS-partner-path-diverges-to-address-business-model-shift?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=062022VAR&utm_content=VAR&Offer=OTHR-youtube_OTHR-video_OTHR-VAR_2022June15_VAR  
What is a VAR:  https://www.techtarget.com/searchitchannel/definition/VAR?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=062022VAR&utm_content=VAR&Offer=OTHR-youtube_OTHR-video_OTHR-VAR_2022June15_VAR  

A value-added reseller, or VAR, is what it sounds like -- a company that resells third-party products with added value. “Added value” often refers to things like software customization, installation services, or professional services like consulting or design. Working with a VAR has many benefits, but some challenges as well. 

Do you buy IT products from a VAR? Do you think the added value is enough to sustain the future of VARs? Share your thoughts in the comments below, and be sure to like and subscribe too.

metadata.title: Value-Added Reseller | The ProfServ Traction Podcast
metadata.author: Steve Preda
metadata.shortDescription:
Tune in to the latest episode of ProfServ Traction Podcast as Steve Preda dives into the world of value-added reselling, uncovering how customization of mainstream software packages can skyrocket profits for businesses like yours.

Time Stamps

[00:15] Steve recalls a client of his — a software developer who was very good at motivating dealers to become committed to distributing software. This client was a value-added reseller, and Steve decided to dive into the concept of value-added reselling 
[00:58] Where value-added reselling comes from — began as a concept from smaller companies which were struggling to sell their software due to the advent of large companies like Oracle and SAP. The smaller companies began to provide integration and customization of the larger companies’ software. In other words, they became value-added resellers
[02:23] Example 1: How Steve’s former client, Zoltan Schwarz, expanded his small company, XAPT through value-added reselling. The company began by implementing Microsoft’s ERP systems for the Hungarian market
[03:15] In 2006, XAPT implemented a customized solution for a Caterpillar dealer. This set off a series of projects to customize solutions for other Caterpillar dealers — ultimately making XAPT an international success. In 2015, they reported a 60% net profit margin
[04:52] How larger companies can be platforms for smaller players to create a very profitable business 
[05:10] Example 2: Steve recalls purchasing a CRM system for his investment bank. This system was a customization of Salesforce for investment banks, but was sold at about 10 times the price of a standard Salesforce CRM license
[06:03] How using customization to create a community for your customers can increase profits
[06:41] How XAPT expanded to three times as large as the original business through value-added reselling
[07:45] Call-to-action to become a value-added reseller and to leave comments

metadata.shortDescription: Shiraz Hasan, VP – AT&T Alliance Channel, sits down with Brian Taney, CEO and Co-founder of GetWireless, to discuss the company’s 25-year journey and longstanding relationship with AT&T. Brian highlights how the AT&T VAR Program creates frictionless experiences through strong support and collaboration, simplifying go-to-market execution. By integrating hardware, software, and services with AT&T connectivity, Brian emphasizes, “Our teams together are able to deliver that complete solution to the end customers” – reinforcing how simplicity, shared expertise, and integrated capabilities are driving customer value and mutual growth.

metadata.title: What the Heck is... a Value-Added Reseller (VAR)?
metadata.author: BrainSell
metadata.shortDescription: As a company evaluating and looking to implement new technology within their organization, why work with a VAR as opposed to directly with the software vendor? Get the answer in this video.

segments.text: Hi everyone. I'm Sarah and welcome to this episode of "What the heck is" -- a
learning with BrainSell video series where we tackle the tough questions and
not so tough questions about running your business. And today I'm joined by
the man the myth the legend and the CEO of BrainSell, Jim Ward. Hi Jim! Hello
Sarah. So Jim, thank you for joining us. Today I asked Jim to be here because
BrainSell is known as a value-added reseller, correct? That's right.
But there's some confusion around what that is. So Jim help us out what the
heck is a value-added reseller? Asked it all the time -- a value-added reseller is
simple. We sell software platforms but then we add value by providing the
services to implement those platforms. That's the value add. So we provide the
training, the implementation, the development, the understanding of
applications of business with technology. Again that's the value add. That makes
sense. So when people come to us or, I hear this question a lot, why wouldn't I
just go directly to the software vendor like a SugarCRM or a Microsoft
and just buy the software from them? Great question, Sarah. You know what
we've found is all those software companies, the vendors, they make the
software and they do a good job at that but they really don't know how to implement
their own software. Some of them might have professional services but again
they're not on the ground day to day with hard parts of the software,
understanding business applications. Our job, which i think is quite different
than the vendor, is to understand what the impact on their business is - the
customer's businesses. How are we gonna impact the customers business with
software? Because software is stupid. It needs to be told what to do. And once we
understand how it affects people in process we come back to the value add.
That's awesome! Thank you Jim for clarifying that for us.
Thank you everyone for joining us for this episode of "What the
heck is." We'll see you next time. bye-bye!

metadata.title: Channel Partner Private Offers in AWS Marketplace
metadata.author: AWS Partner Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Channel Partner Private Offers (CPPO) enables independent software vendors (ISVs) to authorize channel partners (CP) to receive wholesale pricing on software. CPs can extend customized private offers to customers.

Visit the AWS Marketplace Channel Programs page to learn more https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/features/cpprivateoffers

In this demo, learn how a reseller on Amazon Web Service (AWS) Marketplace can create a private offer and apply negotiated contract terms and pricing for a public sector customer or organization. Then learn how a customer accepts the private offer. 

Learn more about AWS Marketplace: https://go.aws/3vNgowk

Contact Us for more Information: https://pages.awscloud.com/awsmp-contact-us.html 

About AWS
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the world’s most comprehensive and broadly adopted cloud platform, offering over 200 fully featured services from data centers globally. Millions of customers—including the fastest-growing startups, largest enterprises, and leading government agencies—are using AWS to lower costs, become more agile, and innovate faster.

AWS in the Public Sector paves the way for innovation and supports world-changing projects in government, education, nonprofit, and healthcare organizations. Check out: https://go.aws/2XV2QeV.

Subscribe to our channel: https://bit.ly/2PQ1wIW
Watch our video catalog: https://bit.ly/38F5Zn1

metadata.title: How Private Offers work on AWS Marketplace explained step by step
metadata.author: Clazar
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how Private Offers work on AWS Marketplace and how ISVs use them to negotiate custom pricing and terms with buyers. In this video, Clazar CEO Trunal Bhanse explains how sellers generate private offers, define buyer-specific terms, and complete deals securely through AWS billing.

You will see how private offers streamline enterprise deals, support multi-year negotiations, and enable channel partner motions through CPPO. This guide is ideal for ISVs looking to accelerate cloud marketplace revenue and close high-value contracts faster.

What this video covers:

What private offers are in AWS Marketplace

How sellers create and configure private offers

How to set custom pricing, terms, and buyer account IDs

How buyers accept private offers

How AWS billing and invoicing works for private offers

When to use private offers for enterprise or volume deals

How CPPO extends private offer capabilities through partners

Clazar helps ISVs automate private offer creation, CPPO flows, and marketplace operations end to end.

segments.text: Hi, I'm Prunal, CEO and co-founder of
Clazar. Kazar helps ISVS streamline and
automate cloud sales and grow revenue on
cloud marketplaces. If you're selling on
the AWS marketplace, you've likely heard
the term private offers. It's a powerful
way to negotiate custom deals directly
with your customers. Let's break down
how they work.
Private offers are essentially
customized contracts that allow you to
set special pricing or terms for
specific customers, all within the AWS
marketplace ecosystem. Here's how they
work. First, you the seller creates a
private offer from your listing in the
AWS marketplace management portal.
Second, you define the buyers account
ID, custom pricing, duration, and terms.
Third, AWS generates a secure private
offer URL that you share with the buyer.
Fourth, the buyer accepts it in their
AWS account console.
And fifth, once accepted, AWS handles
billing, invoicing, and you receive the
payment through the normal dispersement
cycle.
Private offers are essentially useful
for the following. Enterprise customers
requiring tailored pricing and contract
terms. multi-year or volume based deals
or channel partner motions through CPPO
and CPPO is channel partner private
offer which is the channel motion for
AWS.
To sum it up, private offers enable
custom pricing for individual buyers.
AWS still handles billing and payments,
no separate invoicing required. Use them
to close large or strategic enterprise
deals efficiently. And last but not the
least is CPPO extend this concept for
even larger channelled motion that you
have inside the company. [snorts]
Private offers combine the flexibility
of direct negotiation with the trust and
simplicity of AWS billing. They are one
of the best ways to accelerate
enterprise transactions inside of the
AWS marketplace. If you still have any
questions, work with Lazar
implementation expert to launch on AWS
in a couple of weeks or less.

metadata.title: Create AWS Marketplace Private Offers for SaaS Contracts | Amazon Web Services
metadata.author: Amazon Web Services
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, you'll see how to create AWS Marketplace private offers for Software as a Service (SaaS) contracts.
 
With this feature, sellers can offer SaaS products directly to specific buyers, allowing them to negotiate custom prices, payment options, and end user license agreement (EULA) terms for software purchases in AWS Marketplace.
 
For more information on this topic, please visit the resources below:
https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/partners/private-offers

ABOUT AWS
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the world’s most comprehensive and broadly adopted cloud platform, offering over 200 fully featured services from data centers globally. Millions of customers — including the fastest-growing startups, largest enterprises, and leading government agencies — are using AWS to lower costs, become more agile, and innovate faster.

#AWS #AmazonWebServices #CloudComputing #AWSMarketplace #MarketplaceAWS #MarketplacePrivateOffer #AWSPrivateOffer #AWSPO #AWSMarketplacePO

segments.text: In this video, you'll see how to create AWS Marketplace private offers for
Software as a Service (SaaS) contracts.
With this feature, sellers can offer SaaS products directly to specific buyers,
allowing them to negotiate custom prices, payment options, and end user license
agreement (EULA) terms for software purchases in AWS Marketplace.
Before we begin, let’s quickly review the two pricing models supported in
SaaS contract private offers.
The SaaS contract model offers fixed pricing for a defined term and is suitable
for customers who have consistent usage requirements for the SaaS product.
The SaaS contract with consumption model offers a fixed pricing component
combined with additional-usage based pricing for a defined term.
This model is suitable for customers who have variable usage requirements for the
SaaS product, allowing them to pay a base fee while accommodating potential overages.
Now, let's take a look at how sellers can create AWS Marketplace private offers for SaaS contracts.
We’ll begin in the AWS Marketplace management portal, where we're signed
in as a seller, and navigate to our Private offers dashboard.
This list shows all the private offers we’ve created under this account.
We can search for offers and perform actions on selected offers.
We’re going to create a new private offer.
First, we’ll select the product type, which is SaaS.
Next, we’ll select the product offer we want to create.
For the purposes of this video, we’ll offer a SaaS Contract with Consumption.
It can take up to 30 seconds for the offer ID to generate.
Next, we’ll walk through the steps to create the private offer.
Step one is to provide the offer information.
We'll maintain the default offer name, description, and renewal information.
Here, we’ll specify the offer expiration date.
We can save and exit to preserve a draft of our offer at any point.
For this example, we’ll continue through the creation process.
The next step is to configure the offer pricing and duration.
Let’s look at the pricing models we can choose.
We’ll start with Contract pricing with upfront payment.
With this pricing model, we would set a contract price for each contract dimension,
and a unit price for each usage dimension.
The buyer then chooses the desired quantity for each dimension and AWS
invoices the buyer for the full amount upon acceptance of the private offer.
For this example, we’ll use the Contract pricing with installment plan model.
First, we’ll set the contract to start when the buyer accepts the contract
and have a duration of 12 months.
Next, we’ll choose the product dimensions we want to include in the private offer.
If needed, we can add custom dimensions.
Next, we’ll enter the quantity for each dimension.
Since our product type is “SaaS contract with consumption,” we’ll need to specify
a unit price for each usage dimension.
Let’s enter a bulk unit price and apply it to all the dimensions.
Please note that the additional usage section does not apply for a "SaaS
contract only" pricing model.
Next, we’ll enter the total contract price and number of installments.
We’ll set the first invoice date and generate the buyer installment plan.
If needed, we can manually update each invoice amount or date.
The next step is to specify the buyer's AWS account ID so we can target the offer.
We can add up to 23 buyers to this private offer.
On this step, we can configure the legal terms and offer documents.
For this example, we’ll use the Standard Contract for AWS Marketplace.
Now, let's review and create the offer.
The private offer is now being submitted.
We can monitor its progress using the link at the top of the page.
An offer status of "Active" indicates that the private offer is successfully
published and is available for the buyer to accept.
You’ve just seen how to create AWS Marketplace private offers for SaaS contracts.
You can learn more about this topic in the description and links for this video.
Thanks for watching. Now it’s your turn to try.

In this video, you’ll see how to create an AWS Marketplace future dated private offer.

With this feature, buyers and sellers can independently manage the timing of purchases to improve financial planning and streamline the renewal sales cycle.

Future dated agreements, based on accepted private offers, enable buyers to easily pre-book purchases while existing terms are ongoing, provide flexible payment schedules and invoicing to allow buyers to pay for purchases at any time, and enable independent software vendors (ISVs) to authorize Channel Partner Private Offer (CPPO) support.

Learn more about AWS Marketplace at – https://amzn.to/2mpnUu6 
AWS Marketplace is a curated digital catalog that enables Consulting Partners to help their customers find, buy, and deploy the software they need. metadata.title: AWS re:Invent 2024 - Custom pricing: What's new with AWS Marketplace private offers (PEX113)
metadata.author: AWS Events
metadata.shortDescription:
In this lightning talk, AWS Partners learn about the benefits of selling in AWS Marketplace to accelerate their business. Hear how to create and manage private offers with custom pricing and terms for your customers, and details about new features released this year to streamline the private offers user experience. Also explore the several touchpoints that private offers have with AWS Partner Central to connect the dots across your partner journey. This talk is intended for AWS Partners.

Learn more:
AWS re:Invent: https://go.aws/reinvent.
More AWS events: https://go.aws/3kss9CP 

Subscribe:
More AWS videos: http://bit.ly/2O3zS75
More AWS events videos: http://bit.ly/316g9t4

About AWS:
Amazon Web Services (AWS) hosts events, both online and in-person, bringing the cloud computing community together to connect, collaborate, and learn from AWS experts. AWS is the world's most comprehensive and broadly adopted cloud platform, offering over 200 fully featured services from data centers globally. Millions of customers—including the fastest-growing startups, largest enterprises, and leading government agencies—are using AWS to lower costs, become more agile, and innovate faster.

#AWSreInvent  #AWSreInvent2024

metadata.title: Private offer enhancements in Microsoft Marketplace | Partner demo
metadata.author: Microsoft Cloud
metadata.shortDescription:
Watch a guided walkthrough of partner enhancements of private offers in Microsoft Marketplace. Enhancements to private offers simplify purchasing and provide greater flexibility to align eligible private offers with an organization’s timing and business needs.

General availability begins in October 2026. 

Explore Marketplace: https://msft.it/WF_5082500

#microsoft #MicrosoftMarketplace #MicrosoftIgnite

segments.text: Microsoft Marketplace is where we co-build, co-innovate, and co-sell with our partner ecosystem.
Private offers give you the flexibility to structure deals around your customers' needs, from specialized pricing and custom terms to flexible payment schedules.
Let's see how it works by creating a private offer for a SaaS
Before you begin, make sure you have a few things ready.
You'll need an existing public offer in Marketplace, your customer's billing account ID and e-mail contacts, and the name of the customer administrator who can complete the purchase.
With those in place, you're ready to create your private offer.
Sign in to Partner Center.
From the marketplace offers workspace, select Private offers.
Select New Private Offer and give it a name that you and your customer will easily recognize.
For this example, we'll create a private offer with absolute pricing.
First, enter the customer's billing account ID.
Enter a description of the private offer note that this will only be visible to you and your team.
One-step purchasing is enabled by default, simplifying the purchasing experience for your customers.
You can also set future agreement dates for individual plans within your private offer.
If you disable, customers must accept the private offer prior to purchasing for additional governance.
In this example, let's keep One Step Purchasing turned on.
Now, set a date for the offer to expire.
If you've negotiated specific terms and conditions, attach them.
A test if this is a renewal for an existing customer or not.
Add contacts from your organization so they can receive status updates.
Add the e-mail addresses for your customer contacts to let them know the private offer is ready for purchase.
Now we'll add plans choose whether you're selling your own product or another partner's product.
Select Create New Plan and choose from your SaaS products or professional services.
Give the plan a descriptive name and select Add.
Next, we'll configure the pricing, contract length and billing frequency.
Add a plan description, define the contract term length, select the billing cycles and define a price per payment in USD.
You can create a flexible schedule of charges and set market pricing in the currencies supported.
Here you have the option to set the plan to start at a future date.
Setting future dated agreements streamlines renewals to avoid any service gaps.
Before submitting, review the customer, pricing, dates, terms and activation settings.
When everything looks right, select Submit.
Once the private offer is ready, share the link with your customer.
If you added customer contacts, they'll receive an e-mail with a link to review the offer and complete the purchase.
Just keep in mind, the purchase must be completed by someone with the appropriate permissions on the customer's Azure account.
And just like that, you've created a private offer built around your customers' needs.
Once they complete the purchase, you'll be notified and can move forward with the deal.
Private offers through Microsoft Marketplace give you the flexibility to structure the right deal for your customers and turn opportunities into long-term growth.

That's exactly why having this intelligence is absolutely essential for your defense. To arm you properly, here is our road map for today. First, we'll cover the shareholder focused shift, then deconstruct sales methodologies, look at biased TCO and ROI models, vendor circumvention tactics, negotiating under heavy lock-in, and finally key contractual levers. Okay, let's start with section one, the shareholder focused shift from stakeholder value to maximum profit. To really understand the current landscape, we have to look at the massive shift in how software is sold. Historically, you bought perpetual licenses. You paid an upfront cost, had permanent deployment rights, and paid a modest annual support fee. Simple, right? But the industry has aggressively transitioned to mandatory subscription models. This shift effectively strips away your permanent deployment rights, creates massive switching friction, and hands all the pricing power directly back to the vendor. Because once you're heavily reliant on their ecosystem to keep the lights on, they have all the leverage they need to rewrite the rules at renewal time. Moving on to section two, deconstructing sales methodologies inside the vendor's playbook. Let's decode the actual frameworks sales reps are heavily trained on to control the deal. It's like a corporate chess match. First, they try to isolate closing risks and accelerate your internal paperwork so they can bypass pricing negotiations. Then they use value messaging to shape your evaluation criteria, ensuring only their unique proprietary features can win. Finally, they use disruptive selling to maintain high price points. So, what's your countermove? You have to be just as deliberate. Keep your paperwork conditional, strip out their proprietary language in favor of vendor-neutral standards, and strictly enforce your commercial limits. A massive part of that disruptive selling involves manufacturing something called constructive tension. Sales reps are literally coached to push back on your discount requests and challenge your objections. They're relying heavily on your fear of project delays or business disruption. You have to counter this manufactured tension by establishing firm commercial boundaries. You must prove you're entirely willing to reassign the deal to a competitor or delay the project if objective cost targets aren't met. If they sense you won't walk away, there's absolutely no way they're dropping the price. Let's head into section three, biased TCO and ROI models, the financial illusion. Vendors absolutely love providing financial calculators that bundle hard savings and soft savings together into one giant impressive-looking number. But it's a financial illusion. Look at the difference here. Hard budget reductions are actual real cash savings, like completely eliminating an external contract. Soft labor savings, on the other hand, represent fractional time saved by your employees. Unless saving an engineer 4 hours a month directly leads to a measurable headcount reduction or eliminates overtime, it's just a fallacy. It's not going to create actual budget availability for your finance team. So, what does this all mean for your numbers? Standard corporate finance governance requires applying a massive 50% realization haircut to those vendor savings projections. Why 50%? Well, because of implementation delays, adoption friction, and operational leakage. Vendors always assume a perfect 100% realization rate in their models, which conveniently omits the messy reality of how enterprise software is actually deployed. To successfully audit these black box ROI models, you need to ask these exact strategic interrogation questions out loud during your discovery calls. Ask them, "What is your sample size? What historical failure ratios are pre-programmed into this?" Force them to split hard P&L savings from soft labor savings. And finally, ask what realization haircut they've applied. Asking these questions instantly shifts the power dynamic. It shows them you're not just going to blindly accept their engineered math. That brings us to section four, vendor circumvention tactics, the dark arts of bypassing procurement. When you start establishing firm commercial positions, vendors will inevitably try to bypass you to regain leverage. They are coached to manipulate your end users or leverage existing C-suite relationships, trying to get technical champions to declare their software business-critical, so procurement loses all its power. Here is your step-by-step defense against these dark arts. Centralize all vendor access strictly through procurement. Enforce an internal communication freeze across your organization during active negotiations. And institute immediate vendor misconduct penalties, like commercial score deductions, if they attempt any off-channel contact. Next up, section five, negotiating under heavy lock-in, creating counter leverage. So, how do you negotiate when you are deeply embedded in a vendor's ecosystem? Well, sales leadership will simply dismiss uncosted threats of leaving as a total bluff. They know migrating takes a ton of time and money. But, presenting a functional, costed exit pilot running on an alternative platform fundamentally alters the commercial negotiation. It proves you have real technical mobility. This documented alternative is literally the most impactful lever you have to break their pricing power and force a realistic discount. To actually optimize your commercial outcomes here, you absolutely must follow this strict sequence. Before you even whisper the word discount, fix your baseline hardware metrics. Consolidate your workloads to strip out phantom overhead. Then, scope your software bundles strictly to what is needed per cluster. Don't buy premium features for standard environments. Next, present that costed exit pilot we just talked about. Then, and only then, do you negotiate the final discount rate on your newly minimized volume. And our final section, section six, key contractual levers, securing structural defenses. When it's time to execute the contract, you must swap out standard vendor defaults for ironclad structural safeguards to prevent total pricing discretion at your next renewal. Cap their annual price escalator at a hard maximum of 3%. Lock in your net price for future expansion, so they don't hit you with massive list price re-quotes when you grow. Lock your skew mix with explicit downgrade rights, so you aren't forced into premium tiers. And ensure you have a scheduled annual window to reduce your core commitments by 10 to 20% as you retire hardware or migrate workloads. Furthermore, hold them accountable to their own sales pitches. If a vendor uses high-value claims to justify premium pricing, force them to back those claims up contractually. Demand TCO performance remedies, meaning if their projected savings fall below 75% in reality, you get a credit. Enforce automatic fee clawbacks for any SLA platform degradations. And absolutely secure stressed exit run rights, which lock in your bridge rates during a transition period if you ever do need to migrate away. At the end of the day, this is a strategic chess match of corporate economics. When the rules change, and your vendor prioritizes extracting maximum profit over your satisfaction, you just cannot rely on past goodwill. So, ask yourself this critical question. If their loyalty shifts overnight, who is structurally defending your IT roadmap? Tomorrow, make sure your procurement team isn't just reacting, but is proactively armed with this playbook to defend your borders and win the negotiation. Thanks for joining this explainer, and stay focused out there.

metadata.title: How TD SYNNEX Services Help Partners Grow Faster | Partner Services Explained
metadata.author: TD SYNNEX
metadata.shortDescription:
What services does TD SYNNEX actually provide, and how can they help partners scale without adding complexity?

In this podcast, Sophia explores the full TD SYNNEX Services portfolio, from training and financing to configuration, professional services, support, managed services, and circular IT. Learn how partners can expand capabilities, increase capacity, and create long-term recurring revenue while keeping customer relationships front and centre.

Visit the Services Hub to discover how TD SYNNEX Services can help you grow: http://ms.spr.ly/6056aVjwj

segments.text: Hello there, and welcome to this session today on partners and services, and I'm joined by
Sophia from TD SYNNEX.
Sophia?
Hi.
Hi.
So, okay, partners, with partner services, they may not even, the TD SYNNEX even do services,
but you do, so let's start from the beginning.
What services do TD SYNNEX offer?
Yeah, it's a really good point.
I think TD SYNNEX have been well known for product distribution for many, many years.
However, we've been doing services for 25 of those years, so we are very well established
within the services space.
But to break it down, as you said, so we do, I break it down in three sections.
We have what we call pre-deployment, deployment, and post-deployment.
So if I start with the first area, pre-deployment is anything from technical training to financing,
so it kind of sets up the particular deal.
Then we move into deployment, which is configuration, integration, and professional services, which
is really utilizing our skill sets within a particular deal or product or solution.
And then we go to post, which is usually the most exciting, because you go into manage
and support, and that's where you can really build relationships long term than just a
box standard transactional deal.
You're effectively side by side with this particular partner, supporting them through
the life cycle of their product.
And then we have circular IT services, so our refurbishment, recycle, proposition.
So not many people know what we call the services value cycle, but this is something that we've
heavily this year, and you know, trying to really create awareness for our partners around what we offer.
Sophia, the service has been good for 25 years, but doesn't that mean competing with your partners?
It's a great question.
I think a lot of our partners that we supply product with are service providers themselves.
The thing that we love to do is share with them actually how we work with you, not against you.
So for example, I was with a partner a couple of months ago, very large UK partner,
I think a lot of their business is probably 85% services led.
And when I sat with them, I asked from their perspective, who delivers the services on their
behalf? And they said out of all the services that they do, 40% of the services delivered
is directly from themselves.
So you're sitting there thinking, okay, who's delivering the other 60%?
And when I asked the question, they were like, we work with over 300 partners.
So this is one of our largest partners.
They buy a lot of product from us, but they actually outsource a lot of their services
to 300 service providers just in the UK alone.
Just imagine the management of that.
It's quite intense.
So what we try to do is when we inform and educate our partners around the services that
we offer, let us be that central point.
You know, it's that one, I'm not saying the one throat to choke kind of methodology,
but effectively we're your chosen distributor.
Let us be your chosen service provider in the areas that you don't have the capacity
or capabilities to deliver yourself.
Well, actually that brings me perfectly to the next point.
You mentioned things like scale.
How do you deliver these things to such a high scale?
Because of our breadth, we cover services.
My area is specifically services around the European region.
So our services proposition, the reason why we're really good at what we do is because
we have that breadth and that scale.
That's why we're really good at product.
We work with a lot of the largest vendors.
We have the biggest channel partners and we're able to provide them at scale and breadth.
Same with services, effectively, we offer that breadth and that scale.
But alongside that, when we deliver it, we have internal resource, so TD SYNNEX services
people, delivery service people providing those services on behalf of the partner.
But because of the scale, we also hand pick and hand select our service providers.
No one from a large distributor perspective or service provider perspective has the ability to
do all of that global European reach on their own.
They'll need some element of support and that's either going to be what we call
partner to partner.
So that's what we do as TD SYNNEX.
We hand select our partners that we entrust delivering services on our behalf
to areas that we may not have the overarching reach.
But the key point there when it comes to partner to partner and how we work with them is
the accountability area is still on us.
So even if we support a partner in a particular service and we utilise our partner network to
get that done, that's on us.
We've selected that partner, so we would still hand hold that entire solution from end to end.
Okay, so 25 years, this has been honed, this has been refined.
You're working with other people.
You've been working with the partners.
So let's just ask for a case study.
Give me an example of someone that you've done this with.
Okay, great, great question.
So there's one that comes to mind and they've been with us for probably, I'd say about 10 years.
They're a small reseller, SMB reseller, five people in total.
And they started with us, they asked for a five-day Microsoft migration service.
And we obviously delivered that for them and delivered that with them.
What it now evolves to in the relationship 10 years on is this particular partner
has utilised our support services and they've utilised our managed services.
They now are utilising our security managed services, given that we've evolved over time.
And today, right now, we're currently integrating their services managed system
with our own services managed system.
So we're actually being a part of their entire invoicing chain.
Now what that showcases is two things.
One, they started small.
They were small, but they started small.
So they probably wanted to ensure that they could trust our key capabilities and work with us
as we evolve the services for them.
But two, they've had that personal touch of TD SYNNEX,
the one that we talk about, keeping IT personal.
They've worked with the same person throughout their entire service journey with us
and they've built relationships and then they've understood what we do so they trust us.
So I think that probably gives a really good example of a partner that's grown with us
and will most definitely continue to grow with us as we expand our portfolio.
Great. So I'm a partner.
I work with TD SYNNEX.
I want to find out more about the services.
How do I engage?
Many ways.
So as a partner, there's a digital way.
So obviously we have our partner first website.
Everything on there talks about services.
We're actually evolving that more as we get into some of our Keycore technology capabilities.
So if you are a partner that is focused on data center,
on that particular site, there will be prompts from a data center perspective.
These are the services that we offer that might be relevant for you.
So if you're a customer, and then there's every single partner in TD SYNNEX has an account manager.
So these account managers, TD SYNNEX people, they're aware of our services proposition,
but there's also dedicated services input.
So you'll have in each country, there's a dedicated services BDM, dedicated services project management.
Ultimately, reach out if you want to know any more information,
or you might have a particular deal or project that you want support on,
or you just want to know what we do in real time,
and you want us to go through what you do and your strategy and work out how we can align together.
Just give us a call and we will happily engage with a meeting and follow up.
Great.
Okay.
Thank you, Sophia.
That's okay.
And if you want to find out any more about TD SYNNEX's services to their partners,
please reach out to Sophia and team.
Thank you.
Thank you.

**Title Suggestion:** Cloud Cost SHOCKER! 😱 Mastering FinOps for Licensing & SaaS: Stop Wasting Money on Software! 🚀

---

### **Video Description**

Are licensed software and SaaS costs secretly sinking your cloud budget? 💸 It's time to get savvy with **FinOps Licensing & SaaS**! This capability is crucial for understanding and optimizing the massive impact these investments have on your organization's cloud value and cost structure.

In this video, we break down the complexities of buying, managing, and optimizing software in the cloud environment. You'll learn how FinOps teams tackle challenges like:

*   **Vendor Terms & True-Ups:** Understanding organizational agreements, complex contract renewals, secondary metrics charged (like API usage or data stored), and why most licenses allow you to increase payment (**true-up**) but not decrease it (**true-down**) 📈📉.
*   **BYOL vs. Marketplace:** Navigating the tricky compliance rules for **Bring Your Own License (BYOL)** rights versus the convenience (and potential cost duplication) of purchasing SaaS or licenses directly through the cloud provider Marketplaces.
*   **Waste vs. Risk:** We show you how to plan usage to minimize under-deployment ("shelfware"/waste) and avoid the dreaded over-deployment penalties that lead to compliance risks and audits 🛑!

FinOps success depends on teamwork! Learn why deep collaboration with your **Procurement**, **Finance**, and **ITAM/SAM** (IT/Software Asset Management) partners is essential for sharing data, managing renewals, and ensuring effective forecasting of total cost of ownership (TCO) 🤝.

Don't let complex licensing rules drain your resources! Hit the like button and subscribe for more deep dives into optimizing your cloud spend! 👇

***

**#FinOps #SaaS #CloudCostOptimization #SoftwareLicensing #BYOL #ITAM #CostManagement #CloudFinOps**

*(Analysis based on the FinOps Foundation's Licensing & SaaS FinOps Framework Capability excerpt.)*

metadata.title: FinOps for SaaS: Realities of Managing SaaS Value at Danske Bank
metadata.author: FinOps Foundation
metadata.shortDescription:
Danske Bank discovered 3,000 SaaS applications across 22,000 employees and sees roughly 100 new ones appear every month. Scott Beasley shares the ITAM-focused perspective on SaaS sprawl, portfolio rationalization, and the growing complexity of consumption-based pricing.

This lightning talk covers examples of SaaS discovery and real-time identification at enterprise scale, portfolio rationalization from 3,000 applications toward a target of 600–800, consumption-based pricing risks and AI-driven SaaS cost inflation, collaborating across security, finance, procurement, and enterprise architecture, and managing internal AI tool proliferation alongside commercial alternatives.

Speaker: Scott Beasley — Danske Bank

Recorded March 24, 2026 at FinOps X Day London, CodeNode.

Join us at FinOps X: https://x.finops.org
FinOps Framework: https://finops.org/framework

#finopsx #finops #finopsforSaaS

segments.text: I'd now like to introduce Scott Beasley from Danske Bank,
who's one of our ITAM experts in the community.
[Applause]
Scott Beasley: Hey. Yeah, I'm one of the slightly different takes today — I'm very
much ITAM-focused. Don't worry, I am FinOps certified, so I can just about get in. But I
want to give a different perspective on how we're managing SaaS from a Danske Bank perspective.
For those who don't know, Danske Bank is an institution in Denmark — pretty much
like Lloyds or RBS in the British Isles. We cover mostly the Nordics. We have a
presence in Belfast and Northern Ireland. About 22,000 employees.
We have three main IT hubs: Denmark centrally with a nice new headquarters, a huge IT center
in Vilnius, Lithuania, and strong support in India. That means a very complex IT environment.
On top of that, we're in the middle of a massive transformation program, moving from our domestic
data center into AWS. With that comes a huge play around what underpins operational
behavior — and that's SaaS. During COVID, we had a massive SaaS explosion with no visibility.
As an ITAM function, we decided to build a real business case to see what was out there.
Hands up — who's on their SaaS journey now? Who's starting? Who's well into it?
That links to the 90% J.R. mentioned this morning — the next phase of FinOps
practitioner input is around the SaaS environment.
As I set my 2026 objectives, I tried to address what the market was showing. SaaS spend is
growing — and what was scary is that if we did nothing, it would grow about 10%. With the AI mix
on top, it explodes further. And consumption-based metrics make it more complex still.
We're also seeing that because of cloud transformation, a lot of vendors are shifting
from traditional licensing to subscription and SaaS models. Be very careful how you
define "SaaS" in your organization — it has a massive bearing on the numbers.
Over the last two years, we've deployed a global system that identifies SaaS on an almost real-time
basis. The high-volume items like ServiceNow and Salesforce — we knew about those. But the
sprawl was in the business, and it's changing all the time. We see approximately 100 new
applications every month — one or two users just testing, one or two thinking about it,
up to hundreds already consuming. The sprawl sits outside the IT organization, which is
concerning in a highly regulated industry with strict data governance requirements.
Over two years, we found 3,000 applications. The question becomes: how do we get down to the 600
to 800 that makes sense for 22,000 users? We're driving efficiency by looking at duplication,
dormancy, and applying a risk-based approach. We funnel down, pick battles,
and prioritize: where are the top users, what business value do these apps provide,
and how many do we have doing the same thing?
All these kind of constitute the same conversation, the same kind of driving
for the same values. And then we've got the one that's risk and shadow in terms of shadow IT.
This one, I don't particularly agree with. I think we're in, as Danske Bank,
we're in quite a good place. We haven't got kind of 50% not being utilized,
but we are looking at adoption techniques and why certain areas are looking at different adoption
areas. So why have they adopted it more in certain areas than other areas? Is it because of the type
of work they do? Is it because of a fundamental regulatory requirement or things like that, right,
in terms of that? But what we are seeing in his huge duplication across different things, I think,
For example, we found about 25 different whiteboard applications. People come in,
use what they've always used, it's easy via the browser, and they start creating
output. But Teams does it. So we need to start moving users to the standard tool.
Historically, SaaS commercial models were straightforward: buy seats, manage them, review
annually. Now it's shifting to consumption-based — all-you-can-eat, peaks and troughs, adding new
features that drive new expense. And what about new applications with integrated AI that bring
different pricing models? That can inflate costs significantly. This is high risk on our agenda.
You can't do this alone. We've collaborated across the business: security, finance,
procurement, end-user services, enterprise architecture. What we've done is provide
the vehicle — the data — to make the right decisions. We give visibility
across the estate on a regular basis so we can prioritize and connect with the right people.
Finally, we've invested heavily in our own Danske GPT — but we're still seeing proliferation of
ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini. Why? That tells us we need to make Danske GPT valuable enough
that users want to use it, and that's where we can start to restrict the alternatives.
If you want to talk more, I can talk about this all day. Dean tasked me with condensing
two years into 10 minutes. Happy to have a conversation over a coffee or a beer afterwards.
Thanks for your time.

segments.text: PHOps, short for financial operations,
is a comprehensive approach to managing
cloud costs effectively. As
organizations increasingly move their
infrastructure to the cloud,
understanding how to optimize spending
while maintaining performance becomes
critical. This practice combines
financial management principles with
cloud engineering to help businesses get
the maximum value from their cloud
investments. Throughout this
presentation, you'll learn the
fundamental concepts, strategies, and
best practices that make PHOPS an
essential discipline for modern
cloud-based organizations.
PHOps is a cultural practice that brings
together three key groups: finance
teams, technology teams, and business
stakeholders. Unlike traditional IT
management, PHOPS emphasizes shared
responsibility for cloud costs across
the entire organization. The goal is to
make datadriven decisions based on
real-time information, foster
collaboration between departments that
typically work in silos, and
continuously optimize cloud spending.
Think of it as a bridge that connects
the financial accountability of
traditional IT with the dynamic ondemand
nature of cloud computing. By
implementing PHOps, organizations can
move faster, innovate more efficiently,
and maintain complete visibility into
where every dollar is being spent.
FHOPS is built on three fundamental
principles that guide how organizations
approach cloud financial management.
First, teams collaborate and take
ownership of their cloud usage. This
means engineers, developers, and
business units understand the cost
implications of their decisions and
actively work to optimize them. Second,
all decisions are driven by the business
value they create. Rather than cutting
costs arbitrarily, organizations
evaluate whether spending delivers
meaningful returns and support strategic
goals. Third, a centralized PHOPS team
enables and promotes best practices
across the organization. This team
doesn't control spending directly, but
instead provides tools, education, and
frameworks that empower every team to
make cost-effective choices. These
principles ensure that cost optimization
doesn't come at the expense of
innovation or business growth.
The PHOPS life cycle consists of three
iterative phases that organizations
cycle through continuously. The first
phase is in form where you establish
visibility and allocation of cloud
spending. This involves understanding
exactly where money is going, who is
using which resources and how costs are
trending over time. The second phase is
optimize where you identify
opportunities for cost savings and
execute on them. This might include
rightsizing resources, purchasing
reserved capacity or eliminating waste.
The third phase is operate, which
focuses on continuous improvement and
automation of cost management processes.
As you move through these phases, you're
not just reducing costs once, but
building a culture and system that
continuously adapts to changing business
needs and cloud environments. Each phase
builds on the previous one, creating a
cycle of ongoing improvement.
Successful PHOps implementation requires
active participation from multiple
stakeholders across the organization.
Finance teams handle budget planning,
cost forecasting, and financial
reporting, ensuring cloud spending
aligns with overall business objectives.
Engineering teams focus on resource
optimization and technical efficiency,
making architectural decisions that
balance performance with cost. Executive
leadership provides strategic direction
and ensures cloud spending supports
broader business goals. Operations teams
manage daily monitoring and respond to
issues in real time. Procurement teams
negotiate contracts with cloud vendors
and manage relationships with service
providers. Product teams analyze how
much features cost to run and make
informed decisions about product
development. When these stakeholders
work together effectively, organizations
can achieve both innovation and
financial discipline, creating a culture
where everyone understands their role in
managing cloud costs.
There are four primary strategies for
optimizing cloud costs. Right sizing
involves matching your resources to your
actual workload requirements, ensuring
you're not paying for capacity you don't
need. Many organizations overprovision
resources as a safety measure, but with
proper monitoring and adjustment, you
can significantly reduce waste. Reserved
instances allow you to commit to
long-term usage in exchange for
substantial discounts, often 30 to 70%
off on demand pricing. This works well
for predictable steadystate workloads.
Spot instances let you leverage unused
cloud capacity at dramatically reduced
costs. Perfect for flexible fault
tolerant workloads that can handle
interruptions. Finally, storage tiering
involves moving data to the most
appropriate storage class based on
access patterns, keeping frequently
accessed data on fast storage while
archiving rarely used data to cheaper
options. Each strategy addresses
different aspects of cloud spending and
can be combined for maximum savings.
Cost allocation through systematic
tagging is the foundation of cloud
financial visibility. Tags are metadata
labels you apply to cloud resources that
allow you to track spending across
multiple dimensions. Common tagging
strategies include labeling resources by
department, such as engineering or
sales, to understand which business
units drive costs. Project tags help
track spending for specific initiatives
like a mobile app or API development.
Environment tags distinguish between
production, development, and testing
resources, ensuring you're not
overspending on non-production
workloads. Owner tags assign
responsibility to specific team leads or
individuals. Cost center tags map
resources to financial accounting
systems. Finally, created date tags help
track resource life cycle and identify
resources that may have outlived their
usefulness. A well-implemented tagging
strategy transforms raw billing data
into actionable insights, enabling
accurate chargebacks, informed
decision-making, and effective cost
optimization.
Effective monitoring and reporting are
essential for maintaining control over
cloud costs. Cost dashboards provide
real time visibility into spending
patterns, allowing teams to see exactly
where money is going at any moment.
These dashboards transform complex
billing data into understandable
visualizations that highlight trends,
anomalies, and opportunities. Budget
alerts send proactive notifications when
spending approaches or exceeds
predefined thresholds, preventing costly
surprises at the end of the month. Trend
analysis uses historical data to
forecast future spending, helping
organizations plan capacity and budget
more accurately. This forward-looking
approach enables better financial
planning and helps justify budget
requests. Anomaly detection
automatically identifies unusual
spending spikes that might indicate
misconfigurations,
security issues, or unexpected usage
patterns. By catching these anomalies
early, organizations can investigate and
resolve issues before they result in
significant financial impact. Together,
these monitoring and reporting
capabilities create a comprehensive view
of cloud financial health.
Automation and governance work together
to enforce cost discipline while
reducing manual effort. On the
automation side, scheduled resource
shutdown turns off non-production
resources during nights and weekends,
eliminating waste without requiring
manual intervention. Autoscaling
policies automatically adjust capacity
based on actual demand, ensuring you
have enough resources during peak times
while scaling down during quiet periods.
Unused resource cleanup identifies and
removes orphan resources like unattached
storage volumes or idle load balancers
that accumulate over time.
Infrastructure as code treats
infrastructure configuration as software
enabling version control, testing, and
repeatable deployments that prevent
configuration drift and errors. On the
governance side, cost policies
enforcement ensures spending stays
within acceptable bounds through
automated controls. Approval workflows
require management signoff for high-cost
resource provisioning. Resource quotas
prevent any single team or project from
consuming excessive capacity. Compliance
auditing maintains records demonstrating
adherence to financial policies and
regulatory requirements. Together,
automation and governance create a
framework that balances control with
agility.
Organizations implementing PHOps face
several common challenges. Lack of
visibility in complex multi cloud
environments makes it difficult to
understand where money is being spent,
especially when resources span multiple
cloud providers with different billing
models and reporting tools. Cultural
resistance occurs when teams are
reluctant to change established
workflows or take on responsibility for
cost management. Engineers may view cost
optimization as someone else's job,
while finance teams may lack the
technical knowledge to influence
infrastructure decisions. Data
complexity arises from the overwhelming
volume of cost and usage data generated
by cloud platforms. Without proper tools
and processes, this data becomes noise
rather than insight. Finally,
organizations struggle with balancing
speed and innovation against cost
control. Moving too fast can lead to
waste and overspending, but too much
control can stifle innovation and slow
down development. Successful PHOPS
practices address these challenges
through education, tooling, clear
ownership models, and a culture that
values both innovation and financial
responsibility.
A variety of tools support PHOPS
practices across different needs and
budgets. Native cloud tools like AWS
cost explorer, Azure cost management,
and Google Cloud billing are provided
directly by cloud vendors. These tools
offer deep integration with their
respective platforms and are often free
or low cost, making them a natural
starting point for cost management.
However, they typically only work with
one cloud provider. Thirdparty platforms
like cloud health, cloudability, aptio
and cubicost provide unified visibility
across multiple cloud providers,
advanced analytics and automation
capabilities. These enterprisegrade
solutions offer features like custom
reporting, optimization recommendations
and integration with financial systems,
though they come with subscription
costs. Open-source tools like cloud
custodian, infraost, and openost provide
cost management capabilities without
licensing fees. These tools are
particularly valuable for organizations
with technical expertise who want
flexibility and customization. The right
tool depends on your environment
complexity, budget, technical
capabilities, and specific requirements.
Many organizations use a combination of
tools to address different aspects of
cloud financial management.
Starting your PHOPS journey involves
four key steps. First, establish a
baseline by thoroughly understanding
your current cloud spending and usage
patterns. This means analyzing where
money is going, identifying the largest
cost drivers, and documenting existing
processes and ownership. Without this
foundation, you won't be able to measure
improvement. Second, build a cross-
functional team that brings together
finance professionals, engineering
leaders, and business stakeholders. This
team should meet regularly to review
costs, discuss optimization
opportunities, and align on priorities.
Third, implement a tagging strategy that
enables accurate cost allocation and
tracking. Define clear tagging
standards, educate teams on proper
tagging practices, and enforce
compliance through automated policies.
Finally, start small and iterate by
beginning with quick wins that
demonstrate value and build momentum.
Don't try to optimize everything at
once. Instead, focus on high impact
opportunities. Measure results, learn
from the experience, and gradually
expand your efforts. Remember that PHOPS
is a journey, not a destination. The
goal is continuous improvement and
building a culture where cost
optimization is everyone's
responsibility.
If you like this video, hit that like
button and don't forget to subscribe.

content.

metadata.title: (Podcast) Preparing for 2026: Software Licensing, ITAM and FinOps Trends
metadata.author: Eddy Says Hi #EddySaysHi
metadata.shortDescription:
🚀 **Preparing for 2026: The Ultimate Software Licensing & FinOps Survival Guide!** 🛡️

The software world is transforming faster than ever, and 2026 is going to be a huge year of change! Are you ready for the subscription takeover, intense vendor consolidation, and the massive cost volatility driven by AI? 😱 We’re breaking down the essential trends you need to master to protect your budget and stay compliant.

**What You'll Learn in This Video:**

*   **Goodbye Perpetual, Hello Subscription! 👋** 2026 solidifies the subscription model as the only viable route for most enterprise products, meaning vendors have stronger leverage than ever at renewal time. Learn how to prepare commercially now!
*   **FinOps is the New Boss! 💰** Cloud spend optimization is now a board-level priority. FinOps is expanding its influence, demanding unified operating models that combine software, SaaS, cloud, and AI cost management.
*   **The AI Cost Conundrum 🤖:** AI workloads (especially GPU-intensive training) are becoming a major source of cost volatility. We dive into why you need new governance approaches—including AI workload cost modeling and consumption guardrails—to handle these expenses.
*   **Compliance Goes Continuous! 🚨** Forget those episodic software audits! Compliance is quietly evolving through telemetry-based monitoring embedded in contracts (shout out to Red Hat and Broadcom). Real-time consumption data is shaping renewal negotiations, requiring proactive oversight.
*   **Taming the SaaS Sprawl Dragon 🐉:** With subscription models everywhere, SaaS waste is on the rise. Learn why focusing on identity governance, usage-based entitlement rightsizing, and automated provisioning is critical for managing costs.

**Your 2026 Priority Checklist: ✅**
To succeed, organizations must adopt proactive governance and integrated operating models. Focus on strengthening contract governance, building a single operating model that unifies ITAM, FinOps, and GreenOps, and developing robust AI workload cost governance frameworks.

Don't wait until it's too late! Independent ITAM consultancy can help improve visibility, strengthen governance, and identify sustainable cost-saving opportunities across your software, SaaS, and cloud estates.

#SoftwareLicensing #FinOps #ITAM #CloudEconomics #2026Trends #SubscriptionModel #AICostGovernance #SaaSManagement #bedigital #TechTrends

***
*Source Information: This analysis is based on "Preparing for 2026: Software Licensing, ITAM and FinOps Trends" by bedigital, published December 16th, 2025.*

metadata.title: FinOps Explained in 5 Minutes | What is FinOps?
metadata.author: Anglepoint
metadata.shortDescription:
FinOps is a growing discipline that has become increasingly more important for organizations. One of the primary goals of FinOps is to optimize cloud costs and improve operational performance and business value.

This FinOps 101 Lightning Course is a guide to help you get started with cloud cost management.

Access the full course here: https://www.anglepoint.com/blog/lightning-courses/finops-and-cloud-cost-optimization/

Topics covered in the FinOps 101 course:

- Understanding FinOps: What is FinOps? Explore the core principles of FinOps and grasp the foundations that make FinOps a game-changer in today’s digital landscape.
- Why FinOps Matters: Learn how FinOps ensures cost efficiency, promotes transparency, and fosters collaboration across teams, creating a synergy between financial objectives and operational excellence.
- The FinOps Cycle: Learn how the FinOps cycle (Inform, Optimize, Operate) transforms cloud cost management into a dynamic and responsive process.
- Challenges and Solutions: Address the common challenges organizations face when implementing FinOps and discover effective solutions.
- The Future of FinOps: Peek into the crystal ball and explore the evolving landscape of FinOps – including some big developments on the horizon.
- Convergence of FinOps and ITAM: Witness the synergy between FinOps and IT Asset Management (ITAM). Understand how the convergence of these disciplines creates a powerful framework for holistic financial control and governance.

Access the full course here: https://www.anglepoint.com/blog/lightning-courses/finops-and-cloud-cost-optimization/

What is FinOps?

FinOps, a portmanteau of “Finance” and “(Dev)Ops,” is a cutting-edge approach and cultural practice focused on cloud financial management, aiming to maximize business value by aligning engineering, IT, finance, and business teams.

The primary goal of FinOps is to optimize the costs associated with running workloads in the cloud, ensuring that organizations can maximize the value they get from their cloud investments while maintaining financial control.

That said, FinOps is not only about cost savings or finding wastage in the cloud. It also provides visibility for all and seeks to ensure accountability for cloud resources. Teams are encouraged to take ownership of the resources they use and understand the financial implication of the decisions they make. FinOps gives the needed insight into spending patterns, cost drivers, and other metrics that support data-driven decisions.
FinOps also includes governance practices to establish policies and guidelines for cloud resource usage.

Central to FinOps is the collaboration between cross-functional teams, promoting said visibility, best practices, and accountability to the variable spending model of cloud computing. Everyone in the organization, from engineers to finance leaders, takes ownership of their cloud costs.

FinOps & the Iron Triangle

FinOps guides decision-making based on the business value of cloud services. It emphasizes making informed trade-offs between cost, performance, and time to market, ensuring that cloud investments drive optimal value for the organization. This is the Iron Triangle of FinOps.
The three components of the FinOps Iron Triangle are cost, quality, and speed. When organizations focus on one of these components, they must make sacrifices to the others. For example, many organizations want to increase their savings in the cloud, this means they may have to start limiting resources or reducing their flexibility. Or, if you want to be more agile and innovative, you may need to increase your risk or costs to focus on achieving that agility.

Therefore, it's essential for your organization to decide what is most important and how you are going to balance cost, quality, and speed. FinOps brings teams together so that they can choose which trade-offs make sense and where they need to place their focus.

FinOps Crawl, Walk, Run Phases

The Crawl, Walk, Run phases of FinOps are a common way that organizations can measure where they are at in FinOps as a whole, and within certain, individual aspects of FinOps. Each phase symbolizes a level of maturity and capability, with the understanding that an organization progresses through these stages gradually.

Organizations might be in different phases for different aspects of FinOps. For example, a company might be in the Crawl phase for cost allocation and tagging, but it could also be in the Run phase for cost avoidance. It’s okay to be in different phases within different areas of FinOps and different areas of the business. FinOps is modular, it’s meant to accommodate and help organizations work through all challenges.

Discover why SaaS spend is a black hole in FinOps with no tool to scrape it all into a single pane of glass. In this FinOps X interview, Peter Greenshaw shares actionable tips on building a single source of truth, optimizing licenses, working with procurement, and applying a FinOps mindset to SaaS renewals to cut waste and save money.

metadata.author: Schwab Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Cybersecurity companies are a double-edged sword, says Ahmed Khan of @morningstar Wealth. While more cybersecurity companies are being created to fend off cyber threats, evolving AI technology creates more of those threats. Ahmed walks investors through his bear, base, and bull cases for CrowdStrike (CRWD) and Okta Inc. (OKTA) as the cybersecurity space grows. He sees more upside for other firms like Palo Alto Networks (PANW), Fortinet (FN) and ZScaler (ZS).

metadata.title: Episode 16 ASC 606 Principal vs Agent Explained: Gross vs Net Revenue Rules
metadata.author: Jobank CPA
metadata.shortDescription:
Master the ASC 606 / IFRS 15 rules for Principal vs. Agent considerations in multi-party enterprise transactions.

In this episode, we break down:
• Step-by-step framework to evaluate Control before transfer (ASC 606-10-55-36)
• Principal vs. Agent presentation differences (Gross vs. Net Revenue)
• Three primary indicators of control: Fulfillment responsibility, Inventory risk, and Pricing discretion
• Real-world SaaS marketplace example with complete accounting journal entries

📌 Reference Accounting Standards:
- ASC 606-10-55-36 through 55-40
- ASC 606-10-55-37A (Indicators of Control)

#ASC606 #RevenueRecognition #PrincipalVsAgent #GrossVsNet #TechAccounting #CFO #Controllership

metadata.title: ASC 606 Revenue Recognition in Plain English: A CPA's Walkthrough of the 5-Step Model
metadata.author: Accounting: Concierge CPA
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we walk through an overview of ASC 606 Revenue Recognition from Contracts with Customers and introduce the 5-step revenue recognition model in plain English.

This is the first video in a new ASC 606 Revenue Recognition series, so the goal here is not to deep dive every rule, judgment area, or edge case yet. Instead, this video focuses specifically on understanding the overall framework and the logic behind the five-step model.

Using a simple SaaS example, we walk step-by-step through:

1. Identifying the contract,
i2. dentifying performance obligations,
3. determining the transaction price,
4. allocating the transaction price,
5. and recognizing revenue when control transfers to the customer.

We also briefly introduce:

deferred revenue,
accrued revenue / contract assets,
over-time vs point-in-time revenue recognition,
and the core idea behind ASC 606:
Revenue follows performance — not cash.

Throughout the video, we break down the actual language used in ASC 606 and translate it into plain English so you can better understand what the standard is really asking.

The next video in the series is a deep dive into Step 1 — identifying the contract under ASC 606.

see the blog post:
https://myconciergecpa.com/revenue-recognition-asc-606/

#ASC606 #RevenueRecognition #USGAAP #FASB #accounting 

📘 TIMESTAMPS

00:00 — $120,000 Cash but $0 Revenue?
00:26 — Introduction to ASC 606
01:52 — Objective and Scope of ASC 606
02:46 — Revenue Follows Performance — Not Cash
03:22 — Step 1: Identify the Contract
04:46 — Step 2: Identify Performance Obligations
07:14 — Step 3: Determine the Transaction Price
08:25 — Step 4: Allocate the Transaction Price
10:06 — Step 5: Recognize Revenue
11:45 — Why Revenue ≠ Cash
12:40 — Deferred Revenue vs Accrued Revenue
14:30 — Point-in-Time vs Over-Time Revenue Recognition
15:12 — Final Thoughts and Next Videos

It is purchasing ongoing access to the software platform. So, in this case, BigTech has one performance obligation, provide access to the software over the one year subscription period. Step three, it is to determine the transaction price. ASC 606 says the transaction price is the amount the company expects to be entitled to in exchange for transferring goods or services to the customer. Now, let's translate what the standard is really asking. In plain English, how much does the company realistically expect to earn from this contract? And in a lot of real-world contracts, this gets messy. Contracts may include variable consideration or usage-based pricing, discounts, rebates, refunds, which means companies may need to estimate revenue before the uncertainty is fully resolved. Now, let's apply this to our example. Big Tech's contract is about as clean as it gets. It's a fixed fee of 120,000. No bonuses, no rebates, no usage charges. The transaction price is 120,000. Done. Variable consideration is its own rabbit hole, and we're going to dig much deeper into it later in this series. Step four is to allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations. ASC 606 says companies generally allocate the transaction price based on the standalone selling prices of each performance obligation. Now, let's translate what the standard is really asking. In plain English, how much of the total contract price belongs to each separate promise? Because once multiple performance obligations are identified, the company may need to recognize revenue for those obligations at different times. Now, let's apply this to our example. Big Tech only has one performance obligation, provide access to the software platform over 1 year. So, in this case, step four takes about 3 seconds. There is only one promise in the contract, so the entire 120,000 transaction price gets allocated to that single performance obligation. But here is why this step exists. Imagine a contract bundles a software license, a one-time implementation project, and 2 years of premium support. There are potentially three performance obligations. Step four is where the company determines how much of the total contract price belongs to each one because those are services may be delivered at different times, which means the related revenue may also be recognized at different times. Big Tech just happens to be a single promise arrangement, so allocation is basically a non-event. For many real-world contracts, it is not. Step five, recognize revenue. ASC 606 says revenue is recognized when or as the performance obligation is satisfied, meaning when control transfers to the customer. Now, let's translate what the standard is really asking. In plain English, when did the customer actually receive the value? And under ASC 606, there are two ways that this can happen. At a point in time or over time. Point in time means control transfers all at once. Think of it as selling a product, delivering equipment, or handing over inventory to a customer. The customer receives the benefit in a single moment, so revenue is recognized immediately. But other arrangements transfer value continuously over time, and SaaS contracts are a perfect example of that. Now, let's apply this to Big Tech. Sandbox receives the benefit of the software every single day throughout the subscription period. Big Tech is not delivering the entire service on January 1st. It is standing ready and providing access across the entire year, which means the performance obligation is satisfied over time. So, Big Tech recognizes the $120,000 gradually over the 12-month contract period. That works out to be $10,000 of revenue per month. $120,000 divided by the 12 months equals $10,000 per month. Now, this is the part people often get backwards. It is very tempting to assume revenue is recognized when the customer pays, but under ASC 606, payment and revenue recognition are two separate questions. Sunbucks paid the full $120,000 up front on January 1st, but Big Tech recognized zero revenue on January 1st because the cash does not drive the timing. The performance does. Month after month, as Big Tech provides access to the software platform, the revenue gets earned and recognized. So, now we can finally answer the question we started with. Big Tech had $120,000 in the bank on January 1st. Revenue on January 1st? Zero. Because at that point, the company had not yet delivered what it promised. Revenue follows performance, not cash. But, hold on. Where does the cash live? If Big Tech collected $120,000 in cash and recognized zero revenue, where does that money live? In the books. It cannot just float in space. When cash and performance do not happen at the same time, the difference usually ends up in one of two places. One, in deferred revenue, or in accrued revenue. Deferred revenue happens when cash is received before the company performs. The company has the money, but it still owes the customer the goods or services. That makes it a liability, specifically a contract liability under ASC 606. And that is exactly what happened with Big Tech. On January 1st, Big Tech receives the cash, but still owed Sandbox one full year of software access. So, the initial entry would look like this. You debit your cash 120,000, and you credit your deferred revenue 120,000. Accrued revenue is the exact opposite situation. That happens when the company performs first, but cash has not yet been received or billed. Instead of recording a liability, the company records an asset called a contract asset under ASC 606. In practice, many companies also refer to this as unbilled revenue or accrued revenue. If Big Tech had already provided one month of software access before being entitled to bill the customer, the company will record the following journal entry. It will debit contract asset or accrued revenue, and it will credit the revenue account. In this case, the company already performed, but has not yet billed or collected the cash. Same standard, same example, two opposite balance sheet stories depending entirely on whether cash runs ahead of performance or behind it. One more detail worth knowing before we close, because it's easy to miss. It's a natural to assume all software revenue gets recognized over time the way a subscription does. But, ASC 606 isn't really looking at the word software, it's looking at how control transfers. Selling a one-time perpetual license to software the customer controls outright is transferred at a single point in time. Big Tech's ongoing access is over time. Same word, software, two completely different outcomes. That is what ASC 606 is looking for. Look past the label and trace the transfer of control. To wrap it up, ASC 606 took a fragmented set of old rules and replaced them with one consistent framework that works across every industry. ASC 606 can feel overwhelming at first because there is a lot of terminology, a lot of judgment, and a lot of moving parts. But, if you focus on truly understanding the five-step model and the actual language used throughout the standard, everything else starts building from there. Because almost every revenue recognition issue under ASC 606 comes back to the same core questions. What was promised? How much should we recognize? And when was the performance obligation actually satisfied? And in the next video, we're going step-by-step through the framework and then into deeper topics like performance obligations, variable consideration, contracts modifications, and contract assets and liabilities. Thank you for watching, and I will see you in the next one.

Revenue is not recorded when cash arrives. It is recorded when an obligation is satisfied — and AI can help you test whether that timing is conservative or aggressive.

🎓 Financial Modeling and Valuation Course with AI and Excel
https://mnainstitute.com/course/financial-modeling-and-valuation-course/

📌 Under ASC 606 and IFRS 15, revenue follows a 5-step model:
1. Identify the contract
2. Identify performance obligations
3. Determine the transaction price
4. Allocate price to each obligation
5. Recognize revenue as each obligation is satisfied

💡 AI applies directly to revenue quality review in 3 ways:
Upload the 10-K and prompt AI to extract and summarize the revenue recognition footnote — flagging areas where management judgment affects timing.
Ask AI to compare accounts receivable growth to revenue growth across multiple fiscal years using data from Item 8.
Ask AI to extract the unearned revenue balance and flag unusual movement vs prior periods.

🔍 What the analyst still decides:
If AI flags AR growing 30% while revenue grew 15%, you determine whether that reflects a new contract structure — or a deterioration in collections.
AI reduces the hours spent reading. The analyst determines what the pattern means.
