segments.text: Five, how analysts judge the quality of
revenue.
What revenue recognition means?
Revenue is not recorded when cash
arrives in the bank. It is recorded when
a company has fulfilled its obligation
to the customer under the terms of a
contract. This principle is defined by
two closely aligned global standards. In
the United States, the applicable
standard is ASC 606 issued by the
Financial Accounting Standards Board.
Internationally, the equivalent is
IFRS-15, issued by the International
Accounting Standards Board. Both
standards share the same five-step model
for determining when and how much
revenue to recognize. The five-step
model. Step one, identify the contract
with the customer. Step two, identify
the distinct performance obligations
within that contract. Step three,
determine the transaction price, which
is the total consideration expected from
the customer. Step four, allocate that
price to each performance obligation
based on its relative standalone selling
price. Step five, recognize revenue as
each performance obligation is
satisfied. Why timing differs by
business model? The timing of
recognition depends entirely on how and
when those obligations are satisfied. A
software license that transfers control
at a single point in time is recognized
immediately upon delivery. A cloud
subscription that delivers service
continuously over a contract period is
recognized ratably each month over that
period. Microsoft's fiscal year 202510K
states that Office 365 revenue is
recognized ratably over the subscription
period because the cloud services and
desktop applications are treated as a
single integrated obligation.
Analysts read the revenue recognition
footnote first because it reveals
whether a company's timing is
conservative or aggressive.
Part two, product versus service
revenue.
The revenue line on the income statement
is a single number, but it contains
fundamentally different types of revenue
with different risk and predictability
profiles. Microsoft breaks its revenue
into two categories directly on the face
of the income statement. Product revenue
covers perpetual software licenses,
operating systems, gaming hardware, and
other one-time sales. service and other
revenue covers cloud subscriptions
including Azure, Office 365, Dynamics
365, LinkedIn advertising and
consulting. In fiscal year 2025,
Microsoft reported product revenue of 64
billion in service and other revenue of
$218 billion out of total revenue of
$282 billion. Service revenue grew from
180 billion in fiscal year 2024 to 218
billion in fiscal year 2025, a 21%
increase. while product revenue was
essentially flat yearon-year. Recurring
versus non-recurring revenue. Recurring
revenue repeats predictably each period
because customers are locked into
subscriptions or multi-year contracts.
Non-recurring revenue occurs once and
does not repeat, such as a perpetual
license sale or a one-time consulting
engagement. Microsoft's cloud and
subscription revenue is largely
recurring, which means analysts can
project it forward with higher
confidence. Non-recurring items must be
separated out before building a forward
revenue forecast because including them
would overstate the sustainable earnings
base. The detail needed to make this
separation comes from the footnotes and
segment disclosures.
Part three,
acrruel earnings versus cash earnings.
Under acrual accounting, revenue is
recognized when earned, not when cash is
received. This means reported net income
and actual cash generation can diverge
meaningfully in any given period.
Analysts measure this gap by comparing
net income directly to operating cash
flow. In fiscal year 2025, Microsoft
reported net income of $102 billion and
operating cash flow of $136 billion. The
gap here is positive, meaning Microsoft
converted more cash than its reported
profit suggests, which signals strong
earnings quality. The opposite situation
where net income consistently exceeds
operating cash flow is a warning that
profits may not be converting into real
cash. Quality of earnings. Red flags.
Analysts look for several specific
patterns that suggest reported revenue
may not reflect the true state of the
business. The first is accounts
receivable growing significantly faster
than revenue which can indicate that
sales are being recorded before
customers have actually committed to
paying. The second is a sharp spike in
revenue in the final weeks of a quarter.
Sometimes associated with channel
stuffing where distributors accept
inventory before period ends solely to
inflate the reported number. The third
is a growing gap between revenue
reported on the income statement and
unearned revenue disclosed on the
balance sheet which can indicate that
obligations are being closed out earlier
than warranted. Each of these patterns
becomes visible only when the income
statement is read alongside the balance
sheet and the cash flow statement.
Part four, using AI for revenue quality
review.
AI tools can compress the time needed to
locate and compare revenue quality
disclosures across a lengthy annual
filing. One application is uploading the
10K and prompting AI to extract and
summarize the revenue recognition policy
from the footnotes with instructions to
flag any areas where significant
management judgment determines the
timing or allocation of revenue. For
example, you could type summarize
Microsoft's revenue recognition policy
and identify all instances where
management judgment affects the timing
of revenue recognition. A second
application is asking AI to compare
accounts receivable growth to revenue
growth across multiple fiscal years
using the data in item 8. A third is
asking AI to extract the unearned
revenue balance from the footnotes and
flag any unusual movement compared to
prior periods. What the analyst still
decides? AI retrieves the data and
surfaces the patterns. The analyst
decides whether a flagged pattern
reflects a legitimate business change or
a genuine quality concern. For example,
if AI identifies that accounts
receivable grew 30% while revenue grew
15%, the analyst must determine whether
that reflects a new multi-year contract
structure or a deterioration in
collections. Microsoft's 202510K
discloses that payment terms generally
require settlement within 30 to 60 days.
Any sustained shift in receivables
beyond that window would require human
judgment to interpret in full context.
AI reduces the hours spent reading. The
analyst determines what the pattern
actually means.

metadata.title: Revenue Recognition for SaaS Contracts under ASC 606
metadata.author: Ordway
metadata.shortDescription:
Dan Kullback,  CPA and Director of Solutions Engineering at Ordway, explains the importance of revenue recognition for SaaS businesses.  Audited GAAP financials are a critical requirement for raising growth equity, venture debt, and securing other credit arrangements.  Transitioning from cash to accrual accounting is one of the big transitions early-stage SaaS companies need to make as they scale up.

In this episode, Dan shares the background and rationale for the recently introduced ASC 606 standard for US GAAP.  He also explores concepts such as deferred revenue, performance obligations, standalone selling prices, and the other complexities accountants at software companies must consider when making judgments about how to apply the standards.

metadata.author: Jobank CPA
metadata.shortDescription:
Deep dive into ASC 606 Step 1 nuances for SaaS and Tech CFOs, Controllers, and Revenue Accountants. In this video, we break down why informal side letters, latency performance SLAs, and termination clauses turn upfront cash into Refund Liabilities rather than Deferred Revenue.

Key Topics Covered:

ASC 606-10-25-1: Step 1 Enforceable Rights & Contract Terms

ASC 606-10-55-22: Variable Consideration Constraint & Refund Rights

Journal Entries: Refund Liability vs. Deferred Revenue

CPQ & RevOps SOX Internal Controls for Tech Companies

#ASC606 #RevenueRecognition #SaaSAccounting #HybridAI #ARR #ValuationMultiples #TechnicalAccounting #DeferredRevenue #GAAP #PerformanceObligations #CorporateFinance #RevOps #IdentifyingContract

segments.text: Your supplier demands 100% payment
upfront, but your cash is stuck before
the goods even arrive. Here's how to
negotiate better supplier payment terms
and work toward net 30 on net 60 without
damaging the relationship. Let's start.
Understand the payment terms. In
procurement, payment terms determine
when you pay your supplier. For example,
with upfront payment, you pay before the
supplier ships the goods. With net 30,
payment is due 30 days after the agreed
starting point, typically the invoice
date. With net 60, you generally have 60
days from that agreed starting point to
pay. Longer payment terms can improve
your working capital because you retain
cash for longer, but suppliers may
resist because they need cash to
purchase raw materials, pay employees,
and run production. So, the goal isn't
simply to demand longer terms. It's to
make offering those terms commercially
attractive to your supplier. Start with
a smaller request. Imagine your company
purchases $50,000 of components every
month, and the supplier demands 100%
upfront payment. Instead of immediately
demanding net 60, start by proposing a
phased approach. For the next few
orders, you could negotiate 30% upfront
and 70% before shipment. Once you
establish a reliable payment history,
propose net 30. After demonstrating
consistent order volumes and on-time
payments, you can request net 60. This
progression isn't guaranteed, but it
gives the supplier evidence that
extending credit to your company is a
manageable risk. Give the supplier a
reason to agree. Here are three
practical negotiation levers. First,
offer predictable business. If you can
commit to a reliable forecast recurring
orders or mutually agreed volume
commitment, the supplier may be more
willing to discuss longer terms. Second,
demonstrate your creditworthiness. Share
appropriate financial references, trade
references, or credit information that
supports your ability to pay on time.
Third, negotiate a balanced tradeoff.
You might offer consolidated orders,
improve forecast visibility, or longer
term supply agreement in exchange for
better payment terms. For example,
rather than saying, "We want net 60,"
explain that your company can offer
predictable monthly demand and a payment
history in return for gradual extension
of credit. Make sure any volume
commitment is realistic and doesn't
force you to buy unnecessary inventory.
Calculate the working capital benefit.
Let's use our $50,000 monthly purchase
example. If your supplier moves from
upfront payment to net 60, you may
retain cash for longer, potentially
improving working capital. Using a
simplified steady state assumption,
$50,000 monthly purchases times 2 months
equals $100,000.
That represents approximately $100,000
of supplier financing if the full
monthly purchases qualify for net 60 and
the payment cycle is established. Actual
benefits depend on invoice timing,
shipment schedules, credit limits, and
the supplier's agreed terms. Also, don't
ignore the total cost. If the supplier
raises prices or removes discounts in
exchange for longer payment terms,
calculate whether the cash flow benefit
is still worthwhile. Close the
negotiation. Finally, put the agreement
in writing. Confirm the payment trigger,
credit limit, invoice requirements, due
date, treatment invoices, and
consequences of late payment. Most
importantly, don't jump straight from
upfront payment to net 60 if a supplier
has little experience working with your
business. Build trust, demonstrate
reliability, negotiate progressively,
and quantify the financial benefit.
Final takeaway, better supplier payment
terms are earned through a credible
business case, not just a request for
more time. Start with a manageable
change, prove your reliability, and
negotiate toward net 30 or net 60 when
the commercial relationship supports it.
Because effective procurement isn't just
about getting a lowest price. It's also
about managing cash flow and building
sustainable supply relationships. If you
found this video valuable, make sure to
like the video, subscribe to the
channel, turn on notifications. Join our
membership, you will get to break down
supply chain problems and their database
solutions with real-world frameworks
every week. Till then, keep optimizing.
Thanks for watching.

metadata.title: NetSuite Procurement Module: Request for Quote Demo
metadata.author: Bridgepoint Consulting
metadata.shortDescription: Using the Request for Quote (RFQ) transaction within NetSuite Advanced Procurement Module, companies can begin the process of setting up contracts with new and existing vendors. They can analyze which vendor best fits their organizational needs and obtain a better idea related to the pricing and quantity that various vendors can fulfill. In these uncertain times, Request for Quotes (RFQ) will allow a company to have multiple supplier relationships in place in the instance that they are all needed to meet demand, or if a vendor is not able to meet all procurement needs. Contract effective and bid open and close dates on the RFQ ensure timeliness of the vendor submitting their pricing, discounts, terms, and other relevant details.

Vendor Onboarding Process is at the heart of every marketplace managing buyer-seller relationships. This webinar discusses in detail the factors that make a good vendor onboarding process, how can you implement it in your business, vendor onboarding software to use, how to build lasting vendor relationships, and some real-life vendor onboarding and management use cases from marketplace companies. a) Type of onboarding: vendor, agent, partner and many more

metadata.title: The Renewal Illusion: Why Software Vendor Discounts Matter Less Than Data Accuracy
metadata.author: MetrixData 360
metadata.shortDescription:
Is your software renewal discount really a win? In this on-demand webinar, Mike Austin, CEO of MetrixData 360, explains the "renewal illusion": why a negotiated vendor discount can still be a bad deal when the license and usage data behind it is wrong.

A vendor introduces a new pricing model weeks before your renewal. Procurement chases the discount, IT works through the licensing changes, and Finance is asked to approve a number that hasn't been validated. That number often becomes the decision, and this is where enterprise software renewals drift off course.

In this session you'll learn:
- Why discounts don't fix underlying license and spend inefficiencies
- How poor data quality weakens your negotiation leverage before talks even begin
- What to validate before approving your next Microsoft, Oracle or SaaS renewal
- How to move from reactive approvals to informed, data-backed renewal decisions

Who it's for: IT, Procurement, Finance, SAM/ITAM and Vendor Management leaders with a software renewal coming up in the next 3 to 12 months.

More on-demand webinars: https://metrixdata360.com/webinars/
Book a 30-minute call with our licensing experts: https://metrixdata360.com/contact-us/

About MetrixData 360: an independent software licensing and cloud cost advisory firm. We are not a Microsoft partner or reseller. We help enterprises negotiate renewals from their own data, not the vendor's.

#SoftwareRenewal #MicrosoftLicensing #SoftwareAssetManagement

metadata.author: The SaaS CFO
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to SaaS Metrics School, where we break down complex SaaS finance concepts into actionable insights. I’m Ben Murray, The SaaS CFO, and in this episode, we’re diving into a critical – but often overlooked – part of your SaaS business: professional services margins.

If your SaaS company offers onboarding, implementation, training, configuration, or other professional services, it’s crucial to treat it like its own business unit. Why? Because without proper visibility into your services margins, you could be burning cash and not even know it.

✅ In this video, you’ll learn:

♦ What services margin means in a SaaS context
♦ Why you need to format your SaaS P&L to track services revenue and expenses
♦ What benchmark data says about top, median, and bottom performance
♦ Why 15% services margin isn’t terrible – but zero is dangerous
♦ The importance of tracking costs – even if you're not charging for services
♦ How to think about fixed-fee packages vs. hourly billing
♦ The tension between ARR discounts and services revenue
♦ The four key metrics you need to track in your PS function

Running services at a loss may not hurt early on, but as you scale, a money-losing services team will drain valuable cash. Instead, aim for 15%–35% services margins, or even better, 45%–50%, especially if you can productize and package your offerings. But be careful — high-margin services shouldn’t come at the cost of discounted subscription revenue.

🎯 Benchmarks from Ray Rike at Benchmarkit.ai show:

Bottom quartile: 15% services margin

Median: 35%

Top quartile: 50%

Don't let your PS team become a cash sinkhole. Even if services are low-cost or unbilled, they consume real resources, and that cost must be accounted for in your SaaS P&L. You need services revenue in your revenue section and services COGS in your expense section. This setup enables accurate gross profit tracking — and sound decision-making.

If you missed my previous episodes covering professional services metrics like: 

✔ Services Backlog
✔ Monthly Billable Utilization
✔ Forecasting Resource Needs

…go back and watch those to build a complete, scalable PS operating model in your business.

📌 More Resources from Ben Murray – The SaaS CFO

🚀 Subscribe to my daily SaaS metrics newsletter:
https://saasmetricsschool.beehiiv.com/subscribe

📊 Get my SaaS Metrics newsletter:
https://mailchi.mp/df1db6bf8bca/the-saas-cfo-sign-up-landing-page

📈 Join my SaaS Metrics courses:
https://www.thesaasacademy.com/

💡 Become part of my SaaS community:
https://www.thesaasacademy.com/offers/ivNjwYDx/checkout

🔗 Follow me on LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/benrmurray

Whether you're a SaaS founder, CFO, or FP&A leader, understanding your professional services margins is essential for scaling sustainably. Services may not be your core product, but they often shape the customer experience and your cash runway.

📉 If your services margins are negative, it’s time to dig into your P&L structure, pricing, and utilization rates.

📈 If they’re positive and healthy — let’s make sure they stay that way without compromising your ARR.

👉 Comment below: What services margins are you running in your SaaS business?

#SaaSCFO #SaaSMetrics #ProfessionalServices #GrossMargin #SaaSPnL #SaaSFinance #ARR #MRR #Onboarding #Implementation #SaaSCashFlow

metadata.author: The SaaS CFO
metadata.shortDescription:
Today we're diving into an absolutely crucial Professional Services (PS) metric: Billable Utilization. Whether you're operating with fixed-fee scopes or billing time and materials (T&M), understanding billable utilization is critical for running a healthy services organization inside your SaaS business.

👋 I'm Ben Murray, The SaaS CFO. Over the last few days, we've been talking about my Top 4 Professional Services (PS) Metrics.
✅ First, we discussed Services Backlog.
✅ Then, we moved to Services Backlog in Months.
✅ Today, it's all about Billable Utilization (Metric 3 of 4).
✅ And tomorrow, we’ll wrap up with Services Margins.

💬 What is Billable Utilization?
Billable utilization measures the percentage of available hours your professional services staff spend working on billable or project-related activities. It’s vital whether you charge a fixed fee or operate under time and materials engagements.

You must know two things:
✓ How many hours your team is applying to billable projects.
✓ How much available time they have to do so.

It's not just about billing rates or revenue; it’s about ensuring your team is productive without risking burnout.

📐 How Do You Calculate Billable Utilization?
Billable Utilization = (Billable Hours Worked) / (Adjusted Available Hours)

Where: ➤ Billable Hours Worked = hours your team spends on customer projects.
➤ Adjusted Available Hours = the standard full-time hours per year (2080 hours) reduced for PTO, holidays, corporate meetings, training, etc.

By adjusting the denominator, we ensure a realistic target for utilization.

🎯 What’s a Good Target?
Most SaaS PS teams target 70% to 80% billable utilization:
✓ 70%–80% is healthy and sustainable.
✓ Below 70%? It might indicate low backlog or underperformance.
✓ Above 80%? Be careful—you risk employee burnout!

🛠 Why Is Billable Utilization So Important?
✓ It’s critical for services capacity planning.
✓ It helps justify adding new headcount if backlog is building.
✓ It informs budgeting and hiring plans (especially right now during budget season).
✓ It ensures your PS team remains productive without burning out.
✓ It strengthens your SaaS P&L visibility and improves services profitability tracking.

📊 How Does Billable Utilization Connect to Backlog?
If your backlog keeps growing and your services team is consistently in the 70–80% billable range, it's very easy to justify hiring new team members!
This directly ties to revenue forecasting, budgeting, and headcount planning for the next fiscal year.

🚀 Recap: Why You Should Track Billable Utilization
✅ It gives real insights into team productivity.
✅ It prevents overworking and attrition.
✅ It aligns service delivery with financial outcomes.
✅ It supports smart staffing and budget decisions.

👉 Tomorrow, don’t miss it — we’ll talk about Services Margins, the final key Professional Services metric to master.

metadata.title: Effortless SAP Integration with CodeMeter License Central: Scenarios, Benefits, and Key Features
metadata.author: WIBU-SYSTEMS AG
metadata.shortDescription:
Wibu-Systems presents Conversations with Solution Partners: Our talk with INFORMATICS

In this video, experts Ruediger Kuegler, VP Professional Services at WIBU-SYSTEMS AG, and Henry Ritzlmayr, CTO at INFORMATICS Holding GmbH, discuss how SAP integrates with CodeMeter License Central to streamline licensing and subscription models. Discover:  
- The three leading system scenarios between SAP and License Central.  
- How the License Central Connector simplifies integration, reduces costs, and maintains system stability.  
- Implementation strategies for subscription models using SAP and CodeMeter License Central.  
- Key SAP modules in the License Central Connector for efficient communication and data management.  
- Solutions for reseller integration and tailored consulting services to meet unique licensing requirements.  

Learn how this integration enhances operational efficiency and empowers software developers with flexible, scalable licensing solutions.  

👉 Subscribe for more insights on software licensing and integration strategies!

segments.text: So typically, when we speak of an integration of SAP and License Central, there are three different
scenarios. One scenario is: SAP is the leading system, SAP creating all in License Central,
where all the licenses are created - it's a very simple and easy integration and
most of the integrations that we did in the past are using this set. The second option is:
SAP is still the leading system, SAP creates the license, stores the creation of the license,
but later on License Central sends notifications back to SAP about the activation/deactivation
of the lifecycle of the license. And the third scenario, last but not least, is the scenario when
License Portal or License Central is the leading system. And this mainly happens if the user wants
to use subscription models, subscription billing, but SAP is not able to do this. This doesn't mean
that SAP cannot do this, but they cannot set up their SAP system. And in this case, they're using License Central
as the leading system, and then License Central creates an export which can be used to create the bills in SAP.
The LCC connector brings CodeMeter License Central and SAP together. LCC eliminates completely the need of any kind of
interface programming and therefore reduces the duration of typical licensing project and also the
costs significantly. The integration itself doesn't interfere with any kind of standard,
regular SAP business flows and therefore keeps the entire system in a stable state.
For implementations of subscriptions there are three different options. One option is:
SAP triggers the creation of the subscription, and SAP triggers every renewal so every year or
every month, when the subscription is renewed, SAP sends the trigger, SAP creates the bill and we'll
automatically renew the license. The second option is: SAP triggers the creation of a subscription.
And then in License Central renews the license in the background automatically without any trigger,
and we are waiting until we get the cancellation from SAP and then we stop of course the renewal
of the license. This is the second option. And last but not least, the third option is that the
subscription is created in License Central. And then License Central creates a billing
report once a month or once per year, and then this is imported into the SAP system.
And all three solutions are possible and it depends on the capabilities of the existing workflows
of the software developer and how he wants and how we can use utilize the SAP system.
The main three models within the License Central Connector are the communication layer, the dashboards,
and the SAP module integration. The communication layer does not only take care about
the actual communication between CodeMeter License Central and SAP; it's also capable of queuing or
load balancing all the tasks, if the loads either on the network or on the server are high.
As well there is a component like error management tracing or logging. The dashboards bring the data from
CodeMeter License Central to SAP and visualize the connection between the data regarding SAP objects.
This leads to an in-place reporting of both datasets to get the SAP model integration, brings
the licensing process to a specific SAP object like material master, Bill of Material equipment,
just to name a few. License Central Collector is capable of reading the data from those objects
on demand, transferring the data communicating to CodeMeter License Central and, of course,
is also capable of updating those objects based on the results of CodeMeter License Central.
This is a very interesting and important topic because most of the software developers who
sell their software are using their channels, so they are selling via resellers. And typically,
this is a customized project, so if they come to SAP, License Portal and reseller integration,
there are multiple options possible like creating resellers in SAP and pushing them
to the Portal or creating the resellers in the Portal allowing the resellers to create licenses in the Portal
and then reporting back to SAP. So typically, this is an individual project that we implement together with our customers.
As an SAP consulting company, we offer in depth knowledge with all the SAP modules, and as partners of Wibu-Systems
for many, many years, now we gain decent experience when it comes to licensing processes. This gives us the possibility
to support and guide our customers and find feasible solutions for their unique requirements.

metadata.author: The SaaS CFO

If you’re running a Professional Services team in a SaaS company—whether it's onboarding, configuration, training, or implementation—these are the 4 essential metrics you must be tracking from a CFO or corporate finance perspective.

In this episode of SaaS Metrics School, I’m sharing the top metrics I rely on to manage and evaluate a Professional Services (PS) team’s performance and financial health. These KPIs help you understand revenue potential, staffing needs, resource allocation, and profitability within your services org.

📊 What You'll Learn in This Video:
✔️ Metric #1: Services Backlog
Understand how to track the total value of your undelivered services and why this backlog matters for forecasting revenue and managing delivery capacity.

✔️ Metric #2: Backlog in Months
It’s not just about how much backlog you have—it’s about how long it will take to deliver it. Learn how to use "backlog in months" as an operational and hiring signal.

✔️ Metric #3: Billable Utilization
Whether you run a fixed-fee or time-and-material model, tracking billable utilization is key to understanding team efficiency, burnout risk, and bench strength.

✔️ Metric #4: Services Margins
I treat Professional Services like a business within a business. Learn how to calculate and target sustainable services gross margins to drive profitability.

📌 Why These Metrics Matter:

These four metrics provide visibility into the operational efficiency, resource planning, and financial sustainability of your services organization. Whether you're a CFO, VP of Finance, or Head of Professional Services, these are non-negotiables for strong reporting and decision-making.

💬 Yes, there are many other metrics PS leaders track (project delivery timelines, NPS, CSAT, etc.), but from a corporate and CFO lens, these four KPIs offer the strategic insight needed to support growth, drive accountability, and align services with the broader business model.

💥 Upcoming Episodes:

This is just the beginning! In the next four episodes of SaaS Metrics School, I’ll dive deeper into each of these metrics—how to measure them, what tools to use, and how to operationalize them across your org. Subscribe and stay tuned so you don’t miss a beat!

Is your software renewal just a signature on last year’s quote? In this SPK and Associates vlog, Michael Roberts sits down with Sarah Craft, Director of Finance and head of licensing and contracts at SPK, to talk about where companies overspend on software licenses and how to get more value at renewal time.

Sarah has spent the last six or seven years managing licensing for Atlassian, PTC, Microsoft, and GitLab, for customers ranging from 10-user teams to enterprises with 5,000 users. She covers:

Why treating renewals as an admin task instead of a financial decision costs money

Forgotten Atlassian Marketplace apps and unused or over-tiered Microsoft 365 licenses

Why the time to review licensing is before the quote arrives, not after

When bundles like Atlassian Teamwork Collection make sense, and when they don’t

What to consider with PTC’s Creo+ and Windchill+ subscriptions

Planning licenses around growth, system consolidation, and AI usage, not just current headcount

How combining licensing with consulting, implementation, and managed services delivers more total value than a lower price alone

Discover the latest in contracts, risk management, and performance measurement, with a look into future trends and technology. It provides an opportunity for you to stay ahead in the rapidly evolving professional services landscape.

metadata.title: Salesforce License Cost Vs Consultant Cost: Why Consultants Often Cost More Than Licenses
metadata.author: Cloud Trailz
metadata.shortDescription:
Why do Salesforce consultants often cost more than the licenses?

Because you’re not buying the same thing.

In this video, we break down the difference between Salesforce licensing costs and consulting costs and why they don’t scale the same way.

In this video, we cover:
 • What Salesforce licensing actually pays for
 • Why Salesforce doesn’t configure your system for you
 • What you’re really paying for with consultants
 • Why budgeting often misses the consulting piece
 • Alternative ways to manage Salesforce (and their tradeoffs)

Salesforce is a platform.

You pay a subscription to access it.

But that platform doesn’t automatically match your business.

That’s where consultants come in.

They’re responsible for:
 • Configuring the system
 • Aligning it to your processes
 • Building automation and reporting
 • Making it usable for your team

That work takes time.

And that’s what drives the cost.

A lot of companies run into problems because they budget for licenses…

But not for the work required to make Salesforce actually function.

That gap creates confusion:

“Why are we paying more for consulting than the software itself?”

Because the software is the foundation.

The consulting is what makes it work for your business.

There are alternatives:
 • DIY implementation
 • Hiring an internal admin

But those still require time, effort, and ongoing investment.

The real takeaway:

Licenses give you access.

Consulting creates value.

If you’re trying to understand what your Salesforce setup should realistically cost:

👉 Check out more straight answers here: https://www.cloudtrailz.com/buyer-education-hub/

Topics covered:
Salesforce licensing cost
Salesforce consulting cost
CRM implementation
Salesforce setup
Salesforce budgeting

metadata.title: Streamline @Atlassian  Software Licensing & Procurement for Government | Clovity × Carahsoft
metadata.author: Clovity
metadata.shortDescription:
Government agencies must navigate complex procurement rules, contract requirements, and compliance mandates while ensuring operational continuity. Strategic licensing plays a critical role in enabling organizations to adopt Atlassian tools efficiently while staying compliant with public sector procurement processes.

In this podcast, Clovity and Carahsoft experts discuss how government organizations can simplify Atlassian software licensing, streamline procurement workflows, and accelerate implementation through strong partner collaboration.

The conversation explores how agencies can strategically plan, procure, and manage Atlassian licenses while leveraging government contract vehicles to reduce complexity, improve efficiency, and deliver long-term value.

Featured in this Podcast:

Anuj Sachdeva - CEO, Clovity
Cameron Starman - Senior Director of Client Management, Clovity
Kevin Howard Team Manager – Atlassian Practice, Carahsoft Technology Corp.

Topics Covered:

• Strategic Atlassian licensing for government organizations
• Simplifying procurement through contract vehicles
• Co-terming, renewals, and license management
• Navigating public sector procurement cycles
• Leveraging Atlassian marketplace applications
• The role of Clovity and Carahsoft partnership in delivering value

This podcast is part of a series featuring conversations with Atlassian ecosystem leaders discussing digital transformation, licensing strategy, cloud adoption, and modernization across the public sector.

#Atlassian #GovernmentIT #PublicSector #Procurement #LicensingStrategy #Clovity #Carahsoft #DigitalTransformation

metadata.title: The Government's Biggest Software Middleman Exposed
metadata.author: Boring, But Billions
metadata.shortDescription:
On September 24, 2024, the FBI raided Carahsoft Technology Corp - an obscure software middleman making $18.9 billion a year off American taxpayers. But why does the Pentagon need a middleman to buy software in the first place?


In this documentary, we investigate the hidden business of federal software reselling. Carahsoft doesn't write code or manufacture chips, yet they rank as the 20th largest private company in America. By navigating the endless red tape of the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), they became the ultimate tollbooth between Silicon Valley tech giants (like SAP, AWS, and Salesforce) and the U.S. government.

We break down how the government's mandatory open-bidding rules were manipulated through "cover bidding," the chaotic reality of the federal "September Surge" budget deadline, and why the Department of Defense is trapped in a multi-billion-dollar vendor lock-in that they can't turn off—even while under active federal investigation.

If you want to understand how government contracting actually works, how defense budgets are spent on enterprise tech, and the hidden pipelines of government procurement, this is the story of the biggest company you’ve never heard of.

 Chapters:
0:00 - The Tuesday Morning FBI Raid
2:30 - The FAR Compliance Moat (Why the Middleman Exists)
5:16 - The Illusion of Three Bids & Cover Bidding
8:19 - SAP, The September Surge & Burning Budgets
11:12 - The Hostage Machine: Why the Pentagon Can't Leave

Welcome to Boring, But Billions, where we do deep-dive video essays investigating the backend software, hidden vendors, and legacy infrastructure operating behind massive governments and corporations.
🔔 Subscribe for more deep dives into the hidden businesses that run the world.

#Carahsoft #GovernmentSpending #BusinessDocumentary #businessstories  #Economics #DefenseContractors #TechIndustry #BoringButBillions

All materials in these videos are used for educational purposes and fall within the guidelines of fair use. No copyright infringement intended. If you are or represent the copyright owner of materials used in this video and have a problem with the use of said material, please send us an email, boringbutbillions@gmail.com and we can sort it out.

segments.text: Tuesday morning, September 24th, 2024.
It's 8:45 in Reston, Virginia, and
people are just pulling into the parking
lot.
For everyone in town, it's crunch week.
The federal budget year ends on
September 30th.
That means military procurement officers
have 6 days left to spend their leftover
cash. If they don't spend it, Congress
takes it back next year.
Then, a line of unmarked black SUVs pull
straight onto Sunset Hills Road.
>> Potential scheme to over the course of
10 years overcharge the US government
and primarily the Department of Defense
for purchases of SAP technology through
a variety of resellers, including
Carahsoft, that total up to $2 billion.
>> Armed agents step out into the morning
air. Some are wearing blue windbreakers
with yellow FBI lettering. Others work
for the Pentagon's criminal watchdog,
the Defense Criminal Investigative
Service.
They push through the revolving glass
doors with federal search warrants in
hand.
Inside the lobby, sales reps just
freeze.
These agents weren't raiding an
aerospace factory, and they weren't
busting a foreign spy ring.
They were raiding an office that resells
ordinary business software.
The company is Carahsoft Technology
Corporation. They don't manufacture
microchips, and they've never written a
single line of original code. Yet,
Forbes ranks Carahsoft as the 20th
largest private company in the country.
Last year, they booked $18.9 billion in
sales. That's more annual revenue than
Spotify, Airbnb, or DoorDash. Almost
every dime of that cash comes straight
out of American tax dollars. For more
than 20 years, [music] this firm has
been the quiet toll booth for the
Pentagon.
When the military buys cloud [music]
servers or enterprise databases, the
check runs through Reston.
By noon, agents were hauling out
servers, hard drives, and private chat
logs. They were chasing a multi-year
bid-rigging scheme that reached across
94 federal agencies. So, how did an
obscure software reseller corner $18
billion of government spending? And what
did federal investigators actually find
inside the Pentagon's bidding machine?
To understand why this company exists,
start with a simple question. Why
doesn't the military just buy software
directly from Silicon Valley?
If the Air Force needs cloud hosting,
why not just pay Amazon directly? If the
Navy needs databases, why not call SAP
or Microsoft? In commercial business,
that's how things work. In the federal
government, it's practically impossible.
Selling anything [music] to Uncle Sam
means following the Federal Acquisition
Regulation.
Contractors just call it the FAR. It's
more than 2,000 pages of mind-numbing
federal red tape. It controls everything
from accounting systems to labor rules
and domestic manufacturing requirements.
Make one honest paperwork mistake on a
federal contract, and your executives
can face criminal fraud charges.
>> Open markets are predicated on the idea
that if a company harms people,
consumers, workers, and business
partners will choose another option.
We're here today because that choice is
no longer possible.
>> Big tech companies love defense money,
but they hate dealing with government
bureaucracy. They don't want to hire
hundreds of specialized [music]
compliance lawyers just to sell software
licenses. That friction is where a
businessman named Craig Abod saw an
enormous fortune.
Abod graduated with a computer science
degree in 1986.
After spending a decade running another
government contractor, he noticed
something fundamental about the
industry.
Software costs almost nothing to
duplicate, but government paperwork
carries massive friction.
He launched Carahsoft in 2004 to bridge
that gap. His pitch to Silicon Valley
was straightforward. Tech firms could
stay in California and write code, while
Carahsoft would handle all the legal
headaches in Washington.
Carahsoft went out and scheduled prime
contract vehicles like GSA schedules and
NASA SEWP.
These agreements work like pre-approved
catalogs for federal procurement
officers. In return, tech giants gave
Carahsoft master distributor rights.
Carahsoft became the primary pipeline
for SAP, VMware, Adobe, and Salesforce.
The economics were practically
risk-free. Carahsoft bought software
licenses at 40% wholesale discounts,
then sold them to federal agencies at
full catalog prices. On multi-billion
dollar government deals, that margin
piles up fast.
Federal law requires open competition to
stop contractors from gouging taxpayers.
So, how did Carahsoft keep rivals from
undercutting their prices?
Federal procurement rules are designed
to prevent monopolies. Under the
Competition in Contracting Act,
government buyers can't just hand deals
to their favored vendors.
Contracting officers have to follow the
rule of three. That means collecting
[music] at least three independent
competitive bids before awarding a
software contract.
The idea makes complete [music] sense.
When three hungry companies fight for
business, taxpayers get the lowest
price. Except in the government software
market, that competition was largely
staged.
Below Carahsoft sits a wide network of
smaller [music] tech resellers. Many of
them are small firms owned by military
veterans or minorities. Federal agencies
actively seek [music] out these
companies to hit statutory diversity
quotas.
Here's the catch. None of those smaller
firms actually own the software they're
bidding on.
When an Air Force base asks for quotes,
three different resellers might submit
bids, but all three have to call
Carahsoft's quoting desk [music] in
Virginia first.
They all need Carahsoft's wholesale
price before they can calculate their
final numbers.
That setup gave Carahsoft complete
control over the entire bid sheet.
Federal investigators call this
complimentary bidding or cover bidding.
Carahsoft could decide in advance which
reseller was supposed to win the deal.
They'd give that chosen vendor a
favorable wholesale discount.
>> To SAP, the most valuable listed company
in that country, what's going on?
>> Yeah, absolutely, Tom. We got to be
careful around this cuz this is still a
preliminary investigations, but
basically what we understand is the DOJ
is looking into potential potential
price fixing with SAP and Carahsoft,
which is basically a third-party
software provider that kind of is lays
as a liaison between the government and
other people that are bidding for
contracts into software.
>> Then, they'd hand the other two
resellers artificially higher wholesale
quotes. When the contracting officer
reviewed the bids, everything looked
completely legitimate. There were three
separate bids from three different
American companies, but the winning
price had been calculated at the exact
same desk in Virginia.
Taxpayers paid inflated rates while
Carahsoft pocketed the wholesale spread.
Federal prosecutors have seen this
playbook before. [music]
Back in 2015, a former VMware vice
president named Dane Smith blew the
whistle on Carahsoft. He revealed that
Carahsoft was hiding deep commercial
[music] discounts from the government.
While private corporate clients got 60%
off, federal agencies paid near the list
price.
The Justice Department stepped [music]
in, and the company settled for $75
million
without admitting fault.
Carahsoft paid its fine, treated it like
an ordinary cost of business, and kept
expanding.
Meanwhile, a much bigger operation was
already taking shape.
The centerpiece of the current federal
investigation is German software giant
SAP.
Most people assume the military runs on
tanks, ammunition, and jet engines.
Today, the armed forces run on
enterprise resource planning software.
The Pentagon uses SAP databases to
handle military payroll and track spare
parts across global supply chains. If
those databases crash, ships don't sail
and transport planes don't fly.
Carahsoft held the master keys to SAP's
government sales. Between 2014 and 2024,
federal agencies purchased over $2
billion of SAP's technology through
their pipeline.
In 2022, federal prosecutors in Maryland
uncovered evidence that SAP and
Carahsoft were coordinating pricing
across defense contracts. The Justice
Department quickly widened the probe to
include 94 civilian agencies.
Yet despite the scrutiny, federal money
kept pouring into Carahsoft. That's
because of a strange Washington ritual
known as the September surge.
The federal fiscal year ends at midnight
on September 30th. If an agency doesn't
spend its allocated budget by that
deadline, the money disappears. Even
worse, congressional committees will
often cut that agency's budget the
following year.
The system actively penalizes military
leaders who try to save taxpayer money.
As October approaches, federal agencies
scramble to spend tens of billions of
unspent dollars.
But you can't buy an aircraft carrier in
72 hours. But you can buy millions of
dollars of enterprise software licenses
in 5 minutes.
Inside Carahsoft's headquarters, the
sales floor turned into a
round-the-clock trading floor. Hundreds
of young sales reps worked through the
night on headsets. Staff ordered stacks
of pizza and slept on cots between
shifts. They processed government
purchase orders right up until the
midnight cutoff.
The Pentagon relied on Carahsoft because
nobody else could move that much
paperwork that fast.
Federal investigators, however, were
growing furious. For over a year,
Justice Department lawyers demanded
internal pricing sheets, emails, and
transaction logs. Prosecutors argued in
court that Carahsoft repeatedly stalled
and withheld records.
By September 2024, prosecutors ran out
of patience. Six days before the fiscal
deadline, armed federal agents walked
through the front doors. The raid
shocked the defense industry, and it
also revealed a much darker reality.
Normally, when federal agents raid a
corporate headquarters, business grinds
to a halt.
Contracts get canceled, and executives
face emergency congressional [music]
hearings.
None of that happened here.
The very next morning, Carahsoft's
president sent an [music] internal memo
telling employees to keep working.
Across Washington, federal agencies
continued processing payments just like
before.
Why would the Department of Defense keep
paying a company under active federal
investigation?
The answer is simple. The Pentagon has
trapped itself inside a huge digital
hostage machine.
Carahsoft [music] doesn't just resell
SAP databases. They distribute Amazon
Web Services, Google Cloud, Microsoft
tools, and frontline cybersecurity
software from CrowdStrike and Palo Alto
Networks. If the Pentagon suspended
Carahsoft tomorrow, military IT systems
would freeze. Routine software patches
would stop rolling out to frontline
military bases. Servers across the
intelligence community would lose
technical support. The Pentagon can't
fire its middleman because it built an
infrastructure completely dependent on
it.
So, today the federal government is
investigating Carahsoft for fraud while
cutting them billion-dollar checks.
The Maryland antitrust case is still
grinding through the courts, but the
underlying procurement machine hasn't
changed at all. When taxpayers think
about defense spending, they picture
stealth bombers and aircraft carriers.
They rarely think about the invisible
software licenses keeping those weapons
running.
Yet, in a quiet Virginia office park, an
unknown middleman continues [music] to
collect its toll and Washington has no
idea how to turn it off.

metadata.title: What is a GSA Schedule? Learn How to Get on the GSA Schedule, Multiple Award Schedule (MAS) Contract
metadata.author: Federal Schedules, Inc. | FEDSched
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a GSA Schedule? Learn how to get on the GSA Multiple Award Schedule (MAS) contract, eligibility requirements, and proposal submission tips from Federal Schedules, Inc.

TIMESTAMPS:
0:00 - What is a GSA Schedule (MAS Contract)?
0:20 - GSA MAS Contract Structure: Categories, Subcategories & Special Item Numbers (SINs)
0:38 - Prerequisites & Proposal Requirements (Financials, TAA, Past Performance)
1:06 - GSA Proposal Evaluation & 20-Year Contract Terms
1:30 - Timeline, Market Size ($30B+ Annually) & Success Rates
1:55 - GSA Contract Help from Federal Schedules, Inc. (FEDSched)

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
• Definition: A GSA MAS contract is a long-term government-wide contract vehicle that streamlines procurement between commercial vendors and federal buyers.
• Eligibility Prerequisites: Companies must have at least 2 years in business, healthy financial statements, relevant past performance, and TAA (Trade Agreements Act) compliance.
• Contract Scope: A company's products or services must fall within the scope of the GSA MAS Contract, which is broken down into Large Categories, Subcategories, and Special Item Numbers (SINs).
• Value & Duration: Opens access to $30B+ in annual federal spending across up to a 20-year term (5-year base period with three 5-year options).

ABOUT FEDERAL SCHEDULES, INC.:
Since 1986, Federal Schedules, Inc. (FEDSched) has helped companies obtain and manage their GSA MAS contracts. 

Website: https://gsa.federalschedules.com/
Contact Us: https://gsa.federalschedules.com/contact/

This is a video about Trump’s New Executive Order: Will You Need a GSA Schedule to Sell to the Government?

This video discusses a significant executive order signed by President Trump that affects how businesses sell to U.S. federal agencies. The executive order, signed on March 20th, 2025, aims to centralize federal procurement through the General Services Administration (GSA). The video details what this means for businesses, particularly those without a GSA schedule, and the implications for selling common goods and services to the government. It explains the role of the GSA, the potential impact on small businesses, and the timeline for implementation. Practical advice is given for businesses considering applying for a GSA schedule, and additional resources are offered for navigating these changes.

How to track SaaS renewals across every vendor, step by step. Free tracker (no sign-up, exports to your calendar) and free Excel template: https://venduris.com/resources/how-to-track-saas-renewal-dates-across-multiple-vendors
 
Most SaaS trackers hold the renewal date. The date that costs you money comes first: the notice deadline, often 30 to 90 days earlier. Miss it, and the contract renews on the vendor's terms. This tutorial shows the 10 fields every renewal tracker needs, the notice deadline formula for Excel and Google Sheets, a countdown and status column that tells you what to act on first, calendar reminders at 90, 60 and 30 days, and a 30-minute monthly review that keeps it all current.

0:37 The 10 fields your tracker needs

2:21 The 30-minute monthly renewal review
2:33 When a spreadsheet stops being enough
2:49 Recap
 
FREE RESOURCES

What is a SaaS notice period: https://venduris.com/resources/what-is-a-saas-notice-period
How to build a SaaS renewal calendar: https://venduris.com/resources/how-to-build-a-saas-renewal-calendar
SaaS renewal management guide: https://venduris.com/saas-renewal-management

metadata.title: Does Expansion MRR or ARR Include Renewals? | SaaS Metrics School | Renewals
metadata.author: The SaaS CFO
metadata.shortDescription:
Does Expansion MRR or ARR Include Renewals? | SaaS Metrics School | Renewals                      Welcome to another episode of SaaS Metrics School! In today’s session, we’re diving into a question that many SaaS founders, CFOs, and finance teams encounter: Does expansion MRR include renewals? This topic can get confusing, but we’re breaking it down to clarify how bookings, renewals, and expansion all work together in SaaS businesses.

This episode is inspired by a recent student question from my SaaS Metrics Foundation course. We’ll cover key insights into bookings and renewals, and more importantly, how to track them accurately in your SaaS metrics.

Understanding Bookings and Renewals
Let’s start with the basics: When is a renewal considered a booking? When I talk about bookings, I’m referring to executed contracts with customers. In most cases, renewals qualify as bookings when they include net expansion. For instance, if a customer was paying $10,000 a year and renews at $13,000, the additional $3,000 is the expansion booking that goes into your CRM system.

This net expansion impacts your metrics, invoicing, and the overall MRR schedule. The renewal in this case not only renews the current revenue but also contributes to your expansion MRR, affecting important metrics like net dollar retention (NDR) and gross revenue retention (GRR).

When is a Renewal Not a Booking?
On the other hand, if a customer renews at the same rate – for example, paying $10,000 one year and renewing at the same $10,000 for the next year – this is not considered an expansion booking. It’s a flat renewal that counts towards your renewal rate but doesn’t impact your revenue forecast or your retention metrics like NDR or ARR growth.

In this case, while you do track the renewal, it’s not a booking because there’s no net expansion. It’s a flat continuation of the previous contract, which means your MRR schedule remains unchanged.

Renewals & Expansion MRR – How They Interact
So, do renewals affect expansion MRR? As we’ve discussed, they do when there is net expansion. When a renewal involves a price increase, that difference is reflected as expansion MRR, which ultimately boosts your net dollar retention. If the renewal is flat, your MRR schedule remains steady with no impact on expansion MRR, but the renewal still helps maintain your retention rates.

It’s essential to keep these distinctions clear in your SaaS business, especially as you manage complex data flows in your CRM system, billing processes, and MRR forecasting.

Importance of Defining Bookings and Renewals
Understanding when a renewal is a booking and when it isn’t is crucial for maintaining accurate financial forecasting. Misreporting these numbers can lead to faulty revenue projections and skewed SaaS metrics, such as churn, expansion revenue, and overall growth rate. Knowing how to classify renewals, expansion bookings, and recurring revenue correctly ensures your business stays on track.

Final Thoughts
I hope this episode clears up some confusion around renewals and expansion MRR. By understanding the relationship between bookings, renewals, and net expansion, you can better track and manage these key metrics in your SaaS business. If you found this episode helpful, I’d appreciate a five-star rating and review!

If you’re looking to dive deeper into topics like this, make sure to check out my SaaS Metrics Foundation course, where we cover everything from basic metrics to advanced analysis, helping you master the financial side of your SaaS company.

Don't forget to subscribe and hit the notification bell to stay updated on all things SaaS metrics, and check out more episodes of SaaS Metrics School for valuable insights on MRR, ARR, and more.

Thanks for watching, and I’ll see you in the next episode!

metadata.title: Is Your SaaS Spend Out of Control? Here's How To Fix It
metadata.author: Vektorindex
metadata.shortDescription:
Software spend rarely becomes a problem because of one expensive tool.

It becomes a problem through forgotten subscriptions, automatic renewals, duplicate tools, unused seats, unclear ownership, missing renewal dates, and software nobody is actively reviewing.

In this video, we break down how to audit SaaS and technology spend before another renewal hits.

You'll learn how to look for:

• Unused or underused software
• Duplicate and overlapping tools
• Upcoming auto-renewals
• Missing owners and renewal dates
• Vendor concentration
• Contracts and subscriptions that need review
• Technology spending that deserves attention

The goal isn't to blindly cut software.

It's to build enough visibility to make better decisions about what to keep, review, consolidate, renegotiate, or replace.

A proper SaaS spend review should help you answer questions like:

• What are we actually paying for?
• Who owns each tool?
• When does each subscription renew?
• Are we paying for overlapping software?
• Which subscriptions need attention before the next renewal?
• Where is the evidence needed to make a decision?

VektorIndex is building Technology Spend & Renewal Control for businesses that want a clearer view of where their technology money goes — and what needs attention before it leaves.

Learn more about VektorIndex Control:
https://vektorindex.com/control

Subscribe for practical breakdowns of SaaS spending, software renewals, vendor management, technology procurement, and operational control.

#SaaS #SaaSManagement #TechnologySpend #SoftwareCosts #VendorManagement

segments.text: A company can have every software
invoice recorded, reconciled, approved,
filed, and still have no idea what it is
actually paying for. Take this row,
$1,500 a month. What it does not say,
whether anyone still uses it, who
approved it, when it renews, or what
happens if nobody does anything. That
gap between paid and understood, is
where software money quietly disappears.
This video is a walkthrough of how to
close it. A real SAS audit is not a
total. It is a reconstruction. For every
subscription, five questions must have
answers with evidence. What is it? What
does it cost over the full term? Who
owns it and who actually uses it? When
does it renew and how much warning do
you get? And is there a documented
reason to keep it? If any answer is
probably or ask Dan when he is back that
subscription has a control problem
whatever its price.
This matters because the spend keeps
growing. Gartner's 2026 forecast puts
worldwide IT spending at $6.31 trillion
and software is the largest and fastest
growing segment. Industry reporting on
those numbers suggests roughly 9% of IT
budgets is now reserved just to absorb
price increases on software companies
already own. One honesty note, most SAS
waste statistics, including some in this
video are published by companies selling
software management tools. That does not
make them false, but treat them as
directional and check the sources. That
is what we will do throughout.
Unknown software rarely enters through
procurement. It enters through channels
finance can see but does not
interrogate. A departmental card, an
expense claim, a free trial that
converted quietly, a contractor who was
given a seat, a remote team that bought
its own stack. XYO's 2026 index of
enterprise customers found central IT
directly manages only about 15% of SAS
spend. Business lines control the rest.
Bettercloud's 2026 survey reports one in
five organizations found software that
users added or expensed without
approval. Neither figure means your
company is broken. Both mean the default
state of a growing company is drift. The
purchase record and the software reality
slowly move apart. Our fictional example
company Kestrel Freight finds a $29 PDF
tool on a marketing card. A trial that
converted 8 months ago which nobody
remembers authorizing.
$29 does not matter. The failure mode
does. The purchase never passed a
decision point, so there was no owner,
no review date, and no recorded reason.
Multiply that pattern across every card
in the business. Before anyone calls a
license wasted, understand that these
are five different columns. Purchased
seats, what you pay for. Assigned seats,
what is provisioned. Active users, who
logged in within 30 days. Regular users,
who uses it weekly, and business need,
who would actually break if it
disappeared. A subscription can look
healthy in one column and questionable
in another. The industry estimates are
big and they do not agree. XYO says
organizations use about 54% of
provisioned licenses. Verdice analyzing
$30 billion of processed spend calls 14%
fully unused and 51% underutilized.
Gartner has been reported around 30% of
spent. Different methods, different
samples, different definitions, which is
exactly the point. No external number
can tell you what is true inside your
company. These figures say look, they do
not say cancel. An unused seat is a
potential optimization, not confirmed
waste. It might be deliberate spare
capacity, a hire starting Monday,
seasonal staff, or a contractual minimum
you cannot touch. The audit's job is to
attach evidence, usage logs, plus an
owner's confirmation before anyone
touches the contract.
Duplication follows the same discipline.
Companies routinely pay for several
project management platforms, several
CRM, several AI subscriptions at once.
But two tools doing similar things is an
observation, not an instruction.
Consolidation carries migration costs,
training costs, and contractual
commitments. The question is not do they
overlap. It is who owns the overlap,
what would it cost to unwind? And is
either team actually using what they
have. The same logic applies to vendor
concentration. Running many processes on
one platform is often efficient. One
contract, one login, one relationship,
but one renewal date then becomes a
company level event. And your leverage
depends on whether a credible
alternative exists. Concentration is not
bad. It needs to be a known trade-off
with a documented fallback, not a habit
nobody has priced.
Here is the part that costs the most
money. A renewal is not one date. It is
three. The renewal date when payment
triggers, the notice date, the last day
you can signal a change. And the
decision deadline, the moment by which
you must already know what you want,
because after it, the contract renews on
its own terms. In a 90-day notice
contract, the decision deadline sits 3
months before payment. Most tracking
systems record the first date and miss
the other two. The clauses doing the
work are rarely the price. Auto renewal,
notice windows, minimum commitments you
renew into, true-up clauses that bill
for peak usage. Vertic's contract data
suggests a third of SAS contracts let
the vendor raise pricing at renewal. In
some categories, well over half. Watch
what timing does. A $48,000 renewal
discovered a week before payment leaves
no time to check usage, gather evidence,
compare alternatives, or get approvals.
The only available action is paying.
Discover it 120 days out and every
option exists. Rightize, negotiate,
consolidate, even exit. Timing is not
administration. Timing is leverage.
Procurement firms publish consistent
data. The earlier a renewal is opened,
the better the outcome. Their
percentages are vendor data, so treat
them as directional. But a late renewal
is not a negotiation. It is a signature.
Every subscription has up to five
distinct roles. The vendor, the
purchaser, the technical owner, the
budget owner, and the business owner
whose work depends on it. They are
rarely the same person. A subscription
with none of them, an orphaned record,
deserves different treatment from one
with a verified owner. An orphan
subscription is not just possibly wasted
money. It is software with access,
credentials, and data that nobody is
accountable for. This is how zombie
subscriptions survive. Nobody hides
them. A project ends, a contractor
leaves, a team restructures, and because
no process owns the cancellation, the
invoice simply keeps arriving. The fix
is not vigilance. It is structure.
offboarding that covers software, not
just laptops, and a register where every
tool has a named owner asked on a
schedule whether it is still needed.
Which brings us to evidence. This cell,
Adobe 24,00 marketing, the industry
standard for software visibility, and it
answers almost nothing. Where did the
number come from? What period does it
cover? Invoice, card, or contract data?
Is it recurring? Who verified it? A
spend record without a source and a
period is a claim, not a fact.
This is the anatomy of a trustworthy
finding. A finding 66 seats show no
login in 90 days. Evidence: The usage
export dated, a reason it matters. The
renewal window opens in 41 days. A
confidence level high for usage, unknown
for business need, a source, and then a
human decision. Automation can assemble
all of that. It cannot decide whether a
subscription should die. That decision
lives inside business context no system
fully sees. The system surfaces, the
business decides.
Two arithmetic problems quietly corrupt
software reporting. First, currency. If
your teams buy in dollars, euros,
pounds, and rand, a simple sum of
invoice amounts is meaningless until you
state the exchange rate and the date you
apply it. Crossber spend reports need a
declared FX assumption or the total
changes every time the market moves.
Second, annualization. $99 a month is
not $99 a year. It is 11.88 and a
monthly commitment reprices itself every
30 days. Keep four numbers separate:
monthly recurring, annualized, total
contract value, and onetime charges. Mix
them and you will misstate commitments,
sometimes in both directions in the same
report.
Underneath everything sits
normalization. Five spellings of the
same vendor across card statements and
invoices must collapse into one record
or your totals and duplicate detection
are fiction. None of this requires
abandoning spreadsheets. A spreadsheet
is a fine audit tool for a small estate.
The breaking point comes later. Multiple
files, conflicting versions, stale
renewal dates, missing owners, no
history of who changed what. That is
when a spreadsheet stops being a control
system and becomes a place where control
goes to decay. So what does done look
like? Five artifacts, a normalized
ledger, one record per product, one
currency, one period. An ownership map
where every product has a verified owner
or is flagged orphaned. A renewal
calendar tracking the decision deadline
and the notice date, not just payment
day. a findings queue where every item
carries evidence, a reason, a confidence
level, and a source and a decision log.
So, six months later, anyone can see
what was decided, by whom, and why.
Build those five and the audit stops
being a project and becomes a standing
control.
This is the problem we built Vector
Index to solve. The control workflow
takes raw spend data, invoices, card
statements, exports, normalizes it into
one ledger, identifies the vendors, maps
ownership, checks renewal dates and
notice periods, and surfaces the items
that deserve attention, the orphaned
tools, the renewals inside their
decision windows, the seat counts that
do not match usage. Every finding
arrives with evidence, a reason, a
confidence level, and a source, and then
waits for a human decision. We will not
claim a system can tell you whether a
subscription should be cancelled. It
cannot. It identifies what is worth
investigating in order with proof
attached. The business still decides. If
your company has meaningful software
spend and no clear view of what needs
attention, Vector Index Control is built
for exactly that. See how it works at
vectorindex.com/control.
Or take the five questions from this
video, apply them to your 10 largest
subscriptions, and you will already know
more than most companies do.

metadata.author: CSM Practice
metadata.shortDescription:
#SaaSRenewals   #CustomerSuccess #csmpractice

As a SaaS company, reporting your Renewals Forecasts is key. Irit Eizips, CCO and CEO of CSM Practice, shares best practices for reporting on SaaS renewals and forecasts.

To get a better grasp on how companies create SaaS Renewals reports, Irit analyzes Or Guz’s example of a forecast renewal report to help you better understand its components. As we gain understanding through a real-world example, Irit dives into the benefits of SaaS renewals forecast tracking and analysis. 
 
She goes into detail about projected versus estimated SaaS renewals metrics, and how to leverage this information in forecasting quarterly results. 
 
The video includes a few tips on how to improve the renewal process and protect your retention rate, such as:
 
- Code Red process 
- Renewal cohort analysis
- Churn Risk analysis
- SaaS Waterfall Chart 
 
Irit explains each of these concepts and what software tools can be used to implement them.

metadata.title: How Do We Track Retention When We Offer Multi-year Contracts | SaaS Metrics School | Retention
metadata.author: The SaaS CFO
metadata.shortDescription:
Greetings, Ben Murray here! Welcome to another edition of SaaS Metrics School. Today, I’m addressing a crucial question from one of our readers, especially relevant for SaaS companies targeting mid-market and enterprise customers with higher Annual Contract Value (ACV) products.

Reader Question:

"If a SaaS startup has annual contracts, how do you calculate churn each month when not all contracts are up for renewal monthly?"

This is an important topic for those dealing with annual and multi-year contracts. When calculating retention, it’s essential to differentiate between customers locked in contracts and those up for renewal. With higher ACV products ranging from $25k to $200k+ aimed at mid-market and enterprise clients, tracking retention and churn can get tricky.

Key Metrics Discussed:

- Aggregate Revenue Retention: This metric may appear artificially high on a monthly basis because customers are often locked in for a year or more. This can lead to misleading retention figures if we don’t consider contract renewal timing.

- Renewal Rate: Unlike aggregate revenue retention, the renewal rate focuses on customers who are up for renewal and can potentially churn. This is critical for understanding immediate customer behavior and future revenue health.

Why Track Both Metrics? While aggregate retention provides a broad view, renewal rate gives a current snapshot of customer satisfaction and renewal trends. This dual approach allows SaaS businesses to anticipate potential red flags in future retention by analyzing current renewal behaviors.

How to Calculate Renewal Rates:

- Identify customers with contracts up for renewal (annual or multi-year).
- Track the count of accounts and revenue dollars renewing versus those available to renew.
- Use your CRM system to pull this data, aligning it with the anniversary month of each contract.

Importance in Due Diligence:

During due diligence, investors and stakeholders often scrutinize both retention and renewal rates. They’ll question any discrepancies, such as why a particular month’s renewal rate might be significantly lower than the annual retention figure. This highlights the need for detailed, month-by-month tracking of renewal rates.

Conclusion:

If you offer high ACV products, ensure you’re not just tracking customer retention, gross revenue retention, and net revenue retention but also renewal rates. These metrics collectively provide a comprehensive view of your SaaS company’s health, especially when dealing with longer-term contracts.

Thank you for tuning in! I hope this clarifies how to interpret retention and renewal metrics when working with multi-year contracts. Keep those questions coming, and stay tuned for more insights in the next edition of SaaS Metrics School!

Topics Covered:

- SaaS Metrics
- Annual Contracts
- Churn Calculation
- Revenue Retention
- Renewal Rate

- SaaS Financial Metrics

metadata.title: Why Channel Partners Don’t Use Market Development Funds (MDF)
metadata.author: ZINFI Technologies, Inc.
metadata.shortDescription: Have you ever wondered why most partners don’t use market development funds? Our research shows as much as 60% of market development funds are not used each quarter. In this video, we look at a number of reasons for this phenomenon, including partners’ short-term focus, lack of digital marketing expertise, insufficient resources and vendors’ failure to provide tools and marketing concierge services. We also discuss four key steps vendors can take to drive usage rates up.

segments.text: Hello.
Welcome to the ZINFI Technologies Partner Ecosystem Management video series.
Please click on the Subscribe button for informative videos on various aspects
of partner ecosystem management.
Most vendors selling through the channel depend on their partners to generate
demand instead of just relying on leads generated by the vendors.
However, the sad reality is that the channel often remains a fulfillment arm
despite heavy investments that many vendors have made in channel marketing,
particularly in automation and concierge services.
Most partners do not use market development funds or MDF.
In fact,
our worldwide channel survey data shows as much as 60% of market
development funds are not used on a quarterly basis. In this video,
we explore the key reasons why partners are not focused on
selling vendors' products. Most of the time,
partners sell a vendor's product as an alternative to the core solution,
or as an add-on. This scenario is quite common in banking, insurance,
finance, technology, and many other sectors where partners, agents,
resellers, brokers, et cetera,
typically represent multiple vendors in order to provide choices to their client
base.
This lack of primary engagement leads to partners focusing on marketing the
primary solution, but skipping any marketing activities for the add-ons.
As a standalone initiative,
partners tend to focus on the short term.
Most channel partners who generate less than 5 million to 10 million in
annual revenue and lack dedicated marketing resources tend to focus their
business activities on quarterly intervals. However,
we know that effective marketing is not just about running events.
It's about putting together a comprehensive 360 degree approach
tied to inbound and outbound activities. Over the long term,
the focus on quarterly initiatives can cause partners to bypass a structured
approach to marketing, thus failing to apply for market development funds.
Partners do not have digital marketing expertise. In the past,
B2B marketing relied heavily on telemarketing and lead generation,
and B2C marketing depended heavily on advertising. However,
both marketing approaches have changed primarily due to the evolution of social
media, content marketing and social selling activities.
In spite of the changes,
most partners are not equipped properly with the appropriate tools and
techniques to exploit the advantages of digital marketing. Instead,
many partners tend to rely on old techniques like telemarketing and running
events. Partners do not have marketing resources.
It's a well known secret that most channel partners do not have dedicated
marketing resources.
That's one reason they're sometimes called resellers versus re-marketers.
As a result,
most channel partners are not aware of market development funds requirements,
don't know how to apply for them and end up not using them even when they're
available.
Vendors do not provide marketing tools and concierge services.
Many vendors are reluctant to invest in a marketing automation platform that
works for channel partners and offer marketing concierge services.
It is essential today to give channel partners pre-configured campaigns that are
pre-loaded in a channel marketing automation platform. However,
that alone is not enough.
Since many partners do not have dedicated marketing resources,
it is also essential to provide marketing concierge services for free in bite
sizes to those partners who are trying to grow their business,
but struggling due to lack of internal marketing resources.
As you can see,
there is no lack of reasons why a significant portion of vendors' market
development funds (MDF) go unused every quarter.
Vendors can address this problem by taking four key steps.
1. Focus on partners who are using funds.
It is essential to provide partners who are engaged and know how to apply for
funds and get paid with dedicated marketing services agency capabilities
so that partners can quickly apply for funds and execute campaigns that are
aligned with the vendor's business objectives.
2. Eliminate channel corruption.
While this seems like an obvious point in today's business environment,
companies still tend to shy away from addressing this issue. In fact,
they often know which partners are misusing funds,
but don't want to ruffle any feathers. Unfortunately, in some cases,
channel management is also involved in the misuse of funds.
This is where regional or corporate management needs to step in and clean up the
system by bringing in transparency, weeding out corrupt people and partners,
and engaging in a public discussion about why it is essential to use funds properly.
3. Provide channel marketing automation.
As we noted earlier,
campaigns need to be preloaded into a channel marketing automation platform so
partners can quickly search for select and execute campaigns.
The platform needs to be robust enough to provide content in local languages,
and it should make it easy for assets to be customized, co-branded,
and downloadable for execution. Furthermore,
the platform should provide native execution capability so that partners who
want to launch a campaign should be able to do so themselves directly from the platform.
4. Provide marketing concierge services.
Since many partners do not have dedicated marketing resources,
they need to be supported by dedicated concierge services. In much the same way,
direct sales forces need support from marketing teams and indirect sales forces,
aka, the channel.
It can be hard to get partners to use market development funds,
but if vendors provide the proper structure and focus, usage rates will go up.
Vendors who have a clear business objective and purpose and have proper
resources and channel marketing automation in place are not only likely to see
fun utilization rise, but they will also find the return on their channel.
Marketing investments can scale up quite substantially.
Thank you for watching ZINFI Technologies Partner Ecosystem Management video
series. If you've enjoyed this video, please click on the Like button.
Please click on the Subscribe button to stay informed on a variety of best
practices for building a high performing partner ecosystem, using programs,
process, people and technology platforms.
Hope to connect with you soon and have a great day.
