metadata.title: What are Market Development Funds?
metadata.author: Marketing Business Network
metadata.shortDescription:
Market development funds, or MDF, are financial support a vendor makes available to business partners for agreed marketing activities. This clear explainer defines the vendor and partner first, then follows a common reimbursement process from the marketing plan to the reviewed payment.

Follow a fictional software workshop with $1,600 of eligible costs. The vendor agrees to cover half, up to $1,000. See why the approved reimbursement is $800, why the partner covers the other $800, and why a funding limit is different from money actually received.

Learn how receipts and activity evidence support a claim, why approval and deadlines matter, how cash or credits can differ, and why a completed event does not automatically prove new sales. Program terms determine what qualifies and when support is paid.

Sources:
AWS, Funding benefits:
https://aws.amazon.com/partners/funding/
GitLab, Market Development Funds program handbook:
https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/resellers/channel-program-guide/mdf/
AWS Partner Central, Managing fund requests:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/partner-central/latest/getting-started/manage-fund-request.html

Thank you for watching. Like the video and subscribe to Marketing Business Network for more clear business and marketing explainers.

segments.text: What are Market Development Funds?
Market development funds, usually shortened to MDF, are financial
support a vendor makes available to business partners for agreed marketing activities.
A vendor is the company supplying the product.
A partner is another business that helps market or sell it.
The funding might support a workshop, advertising campaign or event
introducing the offering to potential customers.
The purpose is to share the cost of reaching customers.
A common model is reimbursement.
The partner proposes an activity and budget, gets approval, carries out the
activity and submits a claim with supporting evidence.
The vendor reviews that claim and pays the eligible amount under the program rules.
An approved budget is not automatically a payment.
Imagine a software vendor agrees to cover half of a partner's eligible
workshop costs, up to one thousand dollars.
The partner runs a workshop for local business owners.
Its actual eligible costs come to sixteen hundred dollars.
Half of sixteen hundred is eight hundred.
After the claim is approved, the vendor reimburses eight hundred dollars.
The partner covers the other eight hundred.
One thousand dollars was the limit, not a guaranteed payout.
The paperwork explains the difference.
Receipts show what the activity cost.
Invitations, campaign materials, photographs or results can help show what
actually happened, depending on the program.
The partner needs to meet the approval, activity and claim deadlines.
Spending money on an unapproved activity or submitting an unsupported claim
can leave the partner paying the bill.
Program rules vary.
Support can take the form of cash or credits, and a vendor may require the
partner to share the cost.
Reimbursement can also mean paying expenses before the funding arrives.
Partners need to understand which costs qualify, how much support is
available and when payment can happen.
The marketing goal still matters.
A completed workshop is evidence that an activity happened.
It does not by itself prove that the campaign produced new sales.
Track relevant inquiries and later business outcomes separately from attendance and spending.
Funding supports the campaign; it does not guarantee its success.
Think of MDF as support attached to a marketing plan and its conditions.
Follow the chain: approved activity, actual eligible costs, supporting
proof, reviewed claim and payment.
In our example, the vendor and partner share a real cost.
The unused part of the funding limit is not extra profit.
Thank you for watching.
If this helped, please like the video and subscribe to Marketing Business
Network for more clear business explainers.

segments.text: Pause and call your vendor using a known
number before acting on any bank detail
change request. Suppose you receive an
email, appearing to be from a known
supplier, asking to update their bank
details for future payments. (Hypothetical
example.) Criminals may use compromised or
lookalike emails to request changes. The
email thread may look genuine, but that is
not proof. Never trust callback numbers or
contact info in the change request itself.
Use only a previously known or
independently verified number. A
verification workflow reduces risk. Here’s
an illustrative process: pause,
independently call, and require a second
approval. Dual approval and separation of
duties make it harder for a single person
to be tricked by a fraudulent request. If
the vendor confirms the change by phone
using a known number, and a second person
approves, proceed with the payment. If the
vendor denies making the request, do not
process the payment. Report the attempt to
your IT and finance teams. If the vendor
is unavailable, delay the payment until
you can verify through a trusted channel.
If you already sent a suspicious payment,
promptly notify your financial institution
and IT department to try to recall the
funds. Reporting incidents quickly can
help your bank attempt to recall the
funds, but recovery is not guaranteed.
Verification reduces risk but is not proof
an account is safe. Criminals can mimic
threads and contacts. Set clear
organizational policies for verifying all
payment changes, including a multistep
process and dual approval. Train staff to
recognize suspicious requests and follow
the verification workflow every time. To
recap: Pause, verify with a known number,
require dual approval, and report any
suspicious activity promptly. These checks
can reduce risk, but they do not guarantee
a request is genuine. If you suspect a
vendor payment scam, document the incident
and alert your internal teams for
investigation. Do not rely on urgency or
pressure in the email—these are common
tactics used by scammers. If you receive a
payment change request, always check for
subtle differences in the sender’s address
or language. Even if the request fits
previous conversations, always verify
independently. Criminals can access and
mimic old threads. If your business uses
payment platforms, apply the same
verification process for any requested
changes. Keep records of all verification
steps and communications. Documentation
supports investigations and helps prevent
repeat attacks. Review your payment change
policy at least annually and update it as
threats evolve. If your policy requires,
escalate suspicious requests to management
or compliance for further review. Remind
your team: even the best controls are only
effective if followed every time, for
every change. If you identify a scam
attempt, share the information with your
staff to raise awareness and prevent
future incidents. For more information and
updates, review official guidance from
trusted sources like NCUA and the EPA
OIG. This educational video was produced
by SecureOps with Ayden Connor, using
AI-assisted scripting and narration.

metadata.title: You Can't Outsource the Risk: Reg S-P and Vendor Oversight
metadata.author: Ncontracts
metadata.shortDescription:
The SEC's amended Regulation S-P raises the bar on how investment advisors protect customer data — and the compliance timeline isn't moving. In this episode of the Ncast, Rafael DeLeon sits down with Tracy Soehle, Associate General Counsel at the Investment Advisors Association, to work through what the rule demands in practice: building an incident response program, meeting the 30-day notification requirement, and managing service providers in a regulatory environment that still leaves a lot open to interpretation.

For RIAs, this isn't just a compliance exercise. It runs directly through fiduciary duty — and Tracy walks through how firms can meet that obligation while navigating vendor relationships that don't always cooperate.

In this episode:

The two most significant changes in amended Reg S-P: mandatory incident response programs and the 30-day customer notification requirement
Why that 30-day clock is harder than it sounds — and what firms need in place before a breach happens
What "reasonable assurances" from vendors actually means when the rule doesn't require it in the contract
Which service providers will renegotiate and which won't — and how to document the diligence either way
Why you can delegate notification to a vendor but can't delegate the liability
Data mapping as the non-negotiable foundation of the entire program
What SEC examiners are asking for and what "reasonably designed" has to mean in practice

#ncontracts #regulation #regulationsp #sec #investment #dataprivacy  #incidentresponse  #vendormanagement #cybersecuritycompliance

So as you said, the rule was adopted in 2000 and the substance hadn't really changed much since then. But the nature and scale and impact of data breaches has increased substantially. So the SEC wanted to modernize the rule to help protect the privacy of customer data and require firms to notify their clients in the event of a breach. Basically sort of um right in line with basic investment protection principles. >> And and so we're really seeing more of an alignment with financial providers, anyone that is dealing with this type of data in terms of what the regulators are looking for from the federal banking regulators to now the SEC and other other agencies because of a lot of these challenges as you just talked about especially with data breaches and and what is happening and how are vendors using their data as with more plug and play that is going in. So I think again one of the most significant you know pieces of this is this kind of 30-day notification clock. So under the amended rule when a firm becomes aware of an incident involving unauthorized access to sensitive customer information, the clock starts. 30 days to notify affected individuals. That's not a lot of time when you factor in the investigation, the scope, the assessment, the drafting of notification. So Tracy, what are the biggest operational challenges firms face in meeting that timeline? And what should they be doing right now so they're not scrambling when an incident occurs? >> Yeah, the biggest operational challenge with meeting that 30-day timeline is that breaches often take a lot longer than that to investigate and make a reasonable determination about whether breach has actually occurred and then which of your clients may have been impacted. Um I think having a detailed incident response plan and certainly a cross-functional team of people ready to respond to a breach is imperative to meet that that deadline. This can be challenging particularly for small firms um and for firms that outsource IT or use managed service providers. Those vendors need to be able to respond quickly if the firm has a breach. So, in terms of preparation, um you really need to be in touch with any service providers and your cross-functional team and you need to know exactly what you would do in the event of an incident. You You mentioned some of the things that take a long time including drafting a response. Those are the kinds of things that you could um have prepared at least an outline prepared um in advance so that when you're in a situation, you have uh materials at your disposal that'll help you figure out what to do and when you have to notify. >> I I think uh and what you're really talking about here is table top exercises that they could be performing so that they are ready. And I know that um again, I'm going to go back to my knowledge on the banking side. This has really been helpful for those that have done that and especially who is going to say what for the firm. To making sure that there is a consistent message uh and and how they're addressing it, so people are not stepping over each other. It helps to define the lines of control, and who's responsible for what and when. Uh, and how this data is going to be uh, collected. So, I think that there are there are those operational challenges, but that can be soothed uh, like a preparation and training uh, that we we see in this. Uh, but um, I that's the those communication and who's going to handle that are really pretty significant uh, you know, when you're looking at these things. I know that I've had friends that have talked to me after data breach and said, "I got a notification uh, from my institution that there was a breach, but this all started a year ago, and I'm just getting the notification." And I think those are challenges, too, when you know in this day and age like, well, I you know, this happened a year ago, and I'm just getting the notification. It doesn't do a lot to engender trust. So, do you have any thoughts or suggestion when institutions say, "How do we handle that when we're in the midst of an investigation?" >> You know, that's a it's an interesting question. Um, obviously, the rule imposes the 30-day deadline, and it's very specific, I will say, in terms of if you follow a reasonable investigative process, but that process is inconclusive, the rule requires you to notify every client whose data may have been in whatever system was breached. Um, so, it's important to have a cross-functional team that's at the ready and available to you to get that investigation started, and to move as quickly through it as you possibly can. Um, cuz at the end of the day, you will have that 30-day obligation, and although the standard is, you know, when you become aware, um, um, I think that once you once you are aware that, um, there's been some uh access to your system, even if within that 30-day period you can't, um, finish the investigation and conclude for certain that someone's data was compromised, the SEC expectation is that by the end of that 30 days you will file that notification. >> Yeah. So, if I if I have this correct, their the rule includes an exception if you can reasonably determine that the data is unlikely to be misused, the notification isn't required. So, how should firms think about that reasonable basis? And I'm also going to talk about reasonable assurances. And if you could discuss those those differences to the best of your ability. >> Yeah, so, a reasonable basis to believe, um, it's a tough an intention it's an intentionally vague standard, I I I would say. And it's and it is tough for a lot of firms struggle, um, with what is the what what is a reasonable basis. Um, and and as you noted, the rule starts with the premise that you must notify unless, after a reasonable investigation, you determine that sensitive customer information has not or is not reasonably likely to have been used in a way that would result in substantial harm or inconvenience, um, which is also an undefined, um, term. So, it is >> well, let me let me interrupt you there because I'll go into the next question which kind of leads into those reasonable assurances because I think they tie in and we can I think I got the basis that we were talking about there. But, the amended rule requires firms to have written policies and procedures that are reasonably designed to require oversight of the service provider, including thorough due diligence and monitoring. And service providers are now required to notify the covered institution within 72 hours of discovering a breach, so their third party discovering a breach. Uh so my question is, what does reasonable assurance actually mean in contractual terms? And so that's why I just wanted to break it out to make sure. So again, what does reasonable assurance actually mean in terms of connect contractual terms? And are standard vendor questionnaires still sufficient, or does the rule push firms towards something more rigorous? >> Yeah, so nobody knows exactly what reasonable assurances are. And we haven't gotten any guidance from the SEC. Um we do know that there is no requirement that this be in the contract. Um and that is frankly one of the most challenging uh aspects of the rule. When it was originally proposed, the requirement was going to be that advisors had to go back and renegotiate all their contracts. And as I'm sure you're aware, a lot of firms just don't have the leverage um to do that. And so in the final rule, um they did uh take out the requirement that this be contractual. Um so you're sort of left with as most things are in the compliance world, the facts and circumstances determination. Um and so the challenge is that many firms don't have the leverage to get assurances either. So the best they can do is their own diligence, look at what's publicly available, try to have conversations with the vendors to the extent that you can, and then document everything you did to get comfortable that it you can reasonably assume that you will be notified within the 72-hour period. I will say that some of our members uh have taken the approach of notifying the service provider uh uh, of their SP obligations and their expectation that this provider will notify them within the 72-hour period, sort of a negative consent type of process. And some vendors just don't respond, um, but others have responded that they will not commit to that obligation. Um, the first thing you usually hear is, "Well, that rule applies to you, but it doesn't apply to me." Um, and so we're not going to give you, um, you know, we're not going to confirm for you that, uh, within 72 hours, uh, we'll we'll be able to provide you with that notice. Um, and so it's and it's unclear whether, you know, the negative consent process is an acceptable approach, but it's kind of a mosaic, um, and and what you want is a process that you can document that shows that you did all of your investigation, even if the vendor wouldn't, uh, commit to the 72-hour period, that it was reasonable that the vendor, um, will likely notify you. And some of them will say, you know, "We'll work with you, um, but we just can't commit either in writing or verbally that, you know, we'll provide we'll provide you with this notice within 72 hours." >> Um, there's just kind of a fine line there. Are you starting to see or hear from any firms, uh, renegotiate their, you know, their their contract with their service providers to address that notification requirement? I I I realize some may not want to engage, but the same parallel I I use with financial institutions, with banks and credit unions, is that you're in the driver's seat. They are a customer of yours. You have the ability to ask for this is what we're expecting and this is what we're requiring. And if they can't provide it, maybe it's time that you look at another provider. So, let's go back to my first part. Are you seeing that people are making updates in terms of their contracts. >> Where they can, absolutely. Um with vendors that that are willing to renegotiate, um people have gone down that path. There is a very large bucket though of of service providers that will not engage. Their contract is their contract. So, if you're using, you know, a cloud service provider or you're using a popular, um client relationship management software um company or you know, you're using, you know, 365 um the you're not going to be able to uh make any progress with those vendors. And so, the best you can do is diligence and a lot of those vendors have great disclosure on their website that allows you to get comfortable that they're subject to privacy rules and regulations, that they they may even have certifications on their website. Um so, it's Like I said, it's facts and circumstances and kind of the totality of the diligence that you're able to do. Because at the end of the day, if you have uh a major service provider, for example, Office 365, um it's hard to change it's hard to change vendors from an industry standard vendor. >> I on some of those uh yeah, larger vendors as well. Uh but again, to begin thinking about that process and what can we ask for and what should we be asking for? And more so, importantly, what did we ask for that we didn't get a response to? Uh because after every one of these data breaches, we're seeing class action lawsuits. So, um I I'll share something from my kind of days, you know, as an examiner in the banking world. We would often tell uh uh financial institutions that you you know, um you can outsource the function, but you can't outsource the risk. And the SEC really made the same point here that firms can delegate delegate notification to a vendor, but the ultimate responsibility stays with the institution. And that's a powerful statement. And advisory firms are are they internalizing that? Do you see them building that in? >> Oh, absolutely. I mean, you can't outsource fiduciary duty. Um, and so even even in other circumstances outside of of SP, um, when an advisor uses a proxy voting vendor or, um, any other sort of, uh, platform to exercise their obligations as a portfolio manager, um, to a client, then they still retain responsibility for for oversight and and for compliance. And so, um, I think that people are definitely internalizing that obligation. And that's why as they're, um, looking at their risks, uh, in terms of privacy rules and breaches, they're not just looking at their own systems and their own practices, but they're looking at the practices of the service providers as well. >> Right. And, you know, beyond the initial due diligence, there's, you know, requirements to around ongoing vendor oversight. It's part of the kind of entire life cycle that they're looking at. Um, under the uh, and what does, you know, uh, under the amended rule is an annual questionnaire enough or should firms be thinking about more continuous monitoring? Uh, maybe quarterly, uh, or, you know, uh, or yeah. >> Yeah, so the the rule does specifically say that certifications, um, are insufficient. So, in in the adopting release to the rule, um the SEC did give some guidance there. So, you do need to do something more frequently uh than annually, I would think. Um it also depends on the type of service level agreement that you have already with your um service provider. So, for you know, if you're using a a custodian, for example, they probably already have a quarterly process. You probably already get a copy of their um their audit, their SOC 1. Um those are operational items that you can get that again give you comfort. You can still get certifications that we haven't had a breach or with it with some cadence that, you know, works for you, but um just a a simple certification is not going to be enough, and so there is a level of ongoing due diligence um that you'll need to do to to remain comfortable. >> Yeah, and I think some of those things are dependent upon what we're going to talk about because when we talk about all of this vendor oversight, all of this incident response, it depends on knowing what data you have and where it lives. So, let's talk about data mapping. Uh I want you to spend a few minutes on this because I think this is one of those areas where the rules requirements can feel straightforward on paper but get complicated very quickly in practice. You can protect what you don't know you You can't protect what you don't know you have. You can't notify effective in individuals uh if you can't identify them. So, data mapping is found foundational to everything. How should firms approach that exercise, and what do you tell firms uh you know, uh when the honest answer is we're not entirely sure where all of our customer data lives? >> Yeah, I mean, look, it's it it's not required under the rule, as you noted, um but a data mapping exercise to identify customer information, where it resides, who has access it to it, and how is it protected is is really the best approach to compliance, and the SEC has given three outreach seminars um on the topic of SP compliance, and in each and every one of those seminars, they talked about um the types of information they would be requesting during exams, and a data map was one of the first things that they mentioned. Um so, the goal of that exercise is to document um company data inventories and data flows, basically, including information received from other financial institutions, information received from customers, and information provided to your service providers. And that's applicable to both paper and electronic records. Um So, I think data mapping can really facilitate compliance with the requirements because it's hard to imagine uh having a program that's reasonably designed to prevent, detect, correct these types of uh breaches and and then to mitigate and notify when required if you haven't done the exercise of data mapping so that you know where the data is and and who has access to it. >> Yeah. I I I think that is one of these key fundamental areas is knowing who has access to what, and not everybody needs to or should have access to everything. So, the you really understanding where your data resides, and I like to talk to firms that say, you know, your data are the crown jewels of your organization. If that data is exposed or compromised in a data breach, your all of your customers are going to be wondering, "Can I continue trusting this company to protect my data and who I'm dealing with?" Uh there. So, um you know, I I think again you touched on this, but I want to reinforce it. The amended rule broadened the definition of customer information to include data that is held by service providers on the firm's behalf, even if it originated with another financial institutions. So, how are firms handling this expanded perimeter? Do you think they're aware of that from what you hear or do you think they're still learning as we're as we're approaching the dates? >> No, I I think um in my experience, people are definitely uh aware of the requirement. Um I think the trickier one is when you you are hearing or receiving information from another financial institution. An example of that is in the private fund context. So, private funds aren't subject to the rule, um but advisors to private funds are subject to the rule. And so, as an advisor to a private fund, um if you have access from that private fund, which is a financial institution, um to the limited partner list and information about those individuals, then you're actually in scope for the rule. So, you were in scope as a registered advisor to begin with, but your risk goes beyond just the fund as your client if you have information that you've been given from the fund, um and it is information about individuals, then you actually do need to apply Reg SP protections to that data. >> Yeah. And I think this is the other area you know, when we go beyond data, it's on their policies because firms may have individual policies on privacy and other you know, policies on cybersecurity and then still others on vendor management. Uh and usually living in separate silos. Do you have any thoughts how firms can make sure that these the amended rule is reflected holistically across all of these programs? >> I think it starts with a cross-functional approach um to compliance, frankly. Um everything we've heard from the SEC um the the the group within exams the technology team within exams that's examining for um Reg SP compliance, they are looking at all of that holistically. They want to see your cybersecurity policies. They want to make sure that what you're saying in your cyber policy is is, you know, reflected in your your privacy policy and that it's all interconnected and that they don't um conflict with each other. So, it really does start with a cross-functional team of all the stakeholders to help pull together where all that information is and and where it where it resides. Um and then, you know, amend the policies accordingly, but do it across. Um I think that's extremely important because that's one of the first things that we're going to see the SEC looking for in exams. >> So, let's bring this full circle where it really matters examination. When an examiner walks in the door, you know, what does a regulation SP compliance look like in in practice? Uh and the SEC's Division of Examination highlighted Reg SP compliance in its 2026 priorities. Um so, what does a strong answer look like when an examiner walks in the firm uh to to look at their incident response program? >> So, I during the SEC's outreach program for smaller advisers, they actually talked about the types of things that they'd be looking for in exams. They were careful to say, and we've heard from senior SEC officials, we've heard them repeat this publicly, that this is not expected to be a gotcha type of exercise. Um, but in terms of SP compliance specifically, we know that they want firms to provide copies of their policies and procedures, copies of that incident response plan. If you have an IT arrangement or a managed service provider arrangement, they actually want to see the contract. Um, they want you to provide information about the IT governance model, including your committee structures, reporting lines, reporting mechanisms and frequency. They expect to see documentation of any internal investigation regarding privacy specifically or information security issues. They want you to be able to demonstrate that you followed your incident response program. Um, and that you documented it appropriately. They also want to see your risk assessment, which is going to be related to technology, cyber risk, controls, threats, vulnerabilities. That includes that data mapping exercise that we that we talked about. They've consistently said, you know, their common observations that they've cited, including policies and procedures that did not appear to be reasonably designed. So again, you talked about, you know, does the cybersecurity conflict with policy conflict with the privacy policy? They want to make sure that it's tailored to the institution, that it makes sense, and that you're following it internally. They've also said that they've had issues, uh, cited in the exams for, uh, policies and procedures that weren't enforced. So, if you have a written policy, um, and it actually doesn't work for your business because you can't actually follow it, um, that's going to be a problem in exams, as well. And of course, uh, if your policies and things that they're asking for simply do not exist, um, then they're going to have, um, more significant concerns about the about your process. >> Yeah, very true on that in terms of, you know, again, my experience on the banking side and the challenges they're facing there. Um, so, you know, what I looked for when I was examining banks, I didn't want to just see the policy binder. I wanted to see evidence that the program has been tested, that they've had the tabletop exercises, and and especially that the policies are updated. When I would find policies that didn't match what practice was, it didn't give me a lot of faith and confidence in the program that they were doing it. It's just like, you know, or we're we're we're trying to keep up. So, I'd expect the SEC examiners to really take the same, uh, approach. And you shared some of that from what you were hearing from a lot of these last three surveys. Anything to add on that topic? >> You know, um, when they when they did the marketing rule, they went through a process where they, in the exam setting, they, um, interviewed folks and talked to them about what changes they had made to their programs, how had they approached, um, the compliance program as it related to the the new rules, and show them how, um, they had reflected, um, the changes in the policies and procedures, and the timing with which they did that. And to your point, was there training, um, on that on the new policies and procedures? Had they tested all of those policies and procedures? So, it will be an exercise where they conduct a series of interviews um and they are specifically looking to understand how you approached it, the timing of which, you know, you approached it. Um obviously it would be a a concern if if someone had done nothing um you know, the day before the deadline. Um and so, they want to understand what kind of a reasonable process you put in place to make sure that you were addressing all of the requirements. >> And you know, the amended rule did expand on those record-keeping requirements as well that firms need to document compliance with the safeguards and disposal rules uh and retain those records for specified periods. What are some of the practical challenges uh there are for smaller firms? >> Well, for smaller firms, I when you say disposal, that's the hardest part for for smaller firms um cuz they don't throw anything away. >> Right. Right. >> You know, and and see look, some of the larger firms are the are the same. Um so, I think, you know, having to put in place um proper disposal requirements can can be a challenge, particularly when you as most smaller firms do have a lot of outsourced service providers. So, that's a big part of you know, the compliance process to operationalize these amendments is you're going to make sure that your service providers not only are retaining the records that you're you're relying on them to retain for you from a regulatory perspective, but also uh when you terminate that arrangement with that service provider or when the client terminates that there is a reasonable process in place um to dispose of the information when it's no longer required to be kept from a regulatory perspective. >> I think that termination is just also a great point to bring up because most financial institutions are thinking about it from the beginning. What do we have to do due diligence and gather and what do we need to do ongoing, but they're not thinking of it in terms of cradle to grave and what do we do at the end of life there and and who has the data, how are they going to be keeping it? So, I think that's a great point. Tracy, before I let you go, I I want to give you the last word. If you could give one piece of practical advice to a chief compliance officer at a mid-size advisory firm that still has work to do before the June deadline, what would that be? >> Oh, I would say I think muscle memory is the most important element of a timely and thorough response to any compliance breach, privacy breach or otherwise. Um, running table top exercises, training, um, creating an incident response playbook. What steps would we follow if we had a vendor breach? What if it was a denial of service attack and and customer information was involved or a phishing attack that that led to the breach or ransomware. Just having run those exercises to know what steps you would follow make it so much easier for you to respond timely and efficiency um, to certainly a privacy breach because you've got that 30-day deadline, but any other compliance breach for that matter. >> Well, Tracy, I appreciate your time and energy on providing us and sharing with our listeners this very important aspect of regulation SP and as it's hitting these areas, I know it's newer for advisory firms, but again, if you talk to any of your counterparts on the banking side. We've been dealing with it and my sense is we're going to see this throughout all of financial services that is happening because of the data that's out there and what needs to be protected. Um and Tracy, I'll give you just one more shot. Any other last closing thoughts about your organization and what y'all provide? >> Now, the Investment Adviser Association um is as I said uh trade organization that serves um registered investment advisers. We have um lawyers on staff um that, you know, work on all kinds of legal and regulatory compliance issues. Um we have a a database of information that's available. Uh we have a privacy hub, which is a resource uh for members that have, you know, copies of uh sample policies and procedures and checklists, um you know, articles that are written by some of our associate members, which are, you know, um consulting firms and law firms um and and other service providers. So, we have a lot of resources available as you're approaching um your compliance program. And so, we just encourage you to to check us out. >> Great. Well, as we close, I'd like to leave you with you the fact that, you know, keep in mind that you've got to do those uh begin with those risk assessments. Uh you've got to look at the data mapping. You've got to run tabletop exercises you should to really ensure strong preparation and ensure that your policies are consistent with your actual practice. So, that's it for today. Stay compliant and stay focused. Thank you.

Full Playlit on the subject is at https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLE7w6qBn8Hos Master enterprise tech sales strategies to neutralize vendor tactics. Learn the counterplaybook for protecting your organization.

This briefing exposes the psychological and financial maneuvers tech companies use during contract negotiations. We analyze the T.E.A.M. framework and how to effectively deploy anchoring techniques to shift leverage back to the buyer. Whether you are a procurement professional or an executive, understanding these power dynamics is critical for managing vendor relationships.

We also examine the operational impact of SLA penalties and the necessity of defining clear exit rights in your service agreements. By using structured discovery to bypass procurement hurdles, you can avoid unfavorable terms and maintain control over your infrastructure investments. These methods ensure you are not just reacting to vendor demands, but actively defending the enterprise during high-stakes discussions.

segments.text: Welcome to the Explainer. Today, we're
doing something a little different.
We're actually peeling back the curtain
on the high-stakes world of enterprise
tech sales. You know, if you're a buyer,
a procurement pro, or an executive who
signs off on tech infrastructure, you
know exactly what I'm talking about.
Negotiating with these vendors, it can
honestly feel like you're playing chess
against an opponent who can see all of
your pieces. But today, we're handing
you the counter playbook. We're going to
expose the exact, frankly, manipulative
strategies tech companies use to
maximize their profits. And far more
importantly, how you can defend your
organization. Let's dive in.
To really grasp what you're up against
here, you have to hear this mindset. It
comes straight from an actual tech sales
training classroom. Quote, "A budget is
locked in unless it isn't." I mean, wow,
right? When you tell a sales rep your
budget is firmly capped, you probably
think you're setting a hard boundary.
But they are literally trained to view
that as just a flexible obstacle.
They'll push you to siphon funds from
other departments, or they'll even
weaponize the fear of a failed
cybersecurity audit just to force your
hand. They don't take no for an answer.
They just go look for a different door.
Okay, so here's our road map for this
Explainer. First, we'll break down the
tech sales playbook. Then, avoiding the
anchoring trap. Third, calculating total
cost of ownership. Fourth, building your
defense team. And finally, enforcing
real vendor accountability.
Let's kick things off with section one,
the tech sales playbook.
The very second you sit down at the
negotiating table, there are two
violently opposing forces at play. Think
about it. Your procurement team's goal
is to level the playing field, right?
You want to strip away all that
marketing fluff and commoditize the
solution so you can get a strict
apples-to-apples price comparison. But
the tech sales rep, their entire mission
is to dismantle that comparison. They
want to pitch this bundled all-in-one
total solution that you literally can't
break down. And they are actively trying
to bypass your procurement process
altogether.
So, how do they actually pull off this
bypass? Well, it happens surprisingly
early. Reps are heavily trained to
target your user buyers long before a
blind RFP is even a thought. They built
these cozy inside relationships to
essentially coach your team on exactly
what to ask for. They present heavily
bundled solutions. And get this, they'll
even drop preemptive negative
disclosures. That means they're
injecting doubt about a competitor's
features before you've even had a chance
to speak to that competitor. Basically,
by the time procurement officially
enters the chat, the vendor has already
rigged the game in their favor.
Avoiding the anchoring trap.
So, anchoring. It's a classic cognitive
bias. It happens when the initial offer,
and this could be an outrageously high
price, a massive volume commitment, or
even a rigid 12-month contract,
establishes a mental reference point in
your brain.
In situations where you aren't entirely
sure of the exact value, that first
number exerts a massive, almost
gravitational pull over the rest of the
conversation.
If a vendor drops a huge price tag right
out of the gate, everything you
negotiate from that point on suddenly
feels like a win simply because it's
lower than that initial anchor. But, the
reality is you are probably still
drastically overpaying.
So, what's your defense against a
hostile anchor? You unpick it. You do
not just snap back with a defensive
counteroffer. Doing that only validates
their absurd anchor as a legitimate
starting point. Instead, you hit pause.
You need to reframe the value based on
your actual on-the-ground operational
needs. If they insist you absolutely
need their most expensive enterprise
plan, push back. Ask them to justify
exactly which features require that top
tier based on your specific pain points.
Basically, just say no, thank you to
their anchor and completely reset the
board.
And here is the real secret to
high-margin tech deals. The outcome is
usually decided long before a buyer ever
even asks for a discount. Vendors have a
massive toolkit of non-price commercial
levers. Look, if they give you a 15%
price discount upfront, they are going
to silently recoup that margin somewhere
else. They'll slip in aggressive annual
price escalators, auto-renewal clauses
with tiny 90-day notice windows, or
super rigid volume commitments.
Your defense strategy here is incredibly
simple. Recognize that all 12 of the
levers you're looking at right now are
tradeable assets. Never just negotiate
the sticker price. You have to negotiate
the entire commercial structure.
All right, let's jump into section
three, calculating total cost of
ownership.
When you're evaluating a tech vendor,
you really have to look way past that
initial purchase price. You have to look
at the hidden costs that hit you post
signature.
We are talking implementation financing,
intensive staff training, ongoing
maintenance, subscription creep, and
even the eventual cost of data disposal
when you leave. Vendors absolutely love
to highlight these massive ROI claims in
their glossy brochures, but they
completely ignore the unintended
consequences. They ignore the hidden
labor costs and internal resource drains
that your organization is going to
absorb just to make their software
actually work.
To fight back against this, you have to
do what's called demanding the
denominator.
When a tech company hands you a case
study claiming some wild 300% efficiency
gain, look them in the eye and ask,
"Okay, out of how many total customers
analyzed?"
If they dodge that question, they are
showing you a single cherry-picked
composite, not reality.
You have to rigorously audit those ROI
claims, calculate your own hidden
implementation costs, and most
importantly, establish strict kill
conditions for any pilot programs.
If the tech doesn't hit the agreed-upon
metrics within that pilot, you kill it.

metadata.title: Third-Party Risk II: Vendor Monitoring and Rules of Engagement | CompTIA Security+ SY0-801
metadata.author: DevOps Simplified
metadata.shortDescription:
Quillmere's payroll vendor sent a SOC 2 report whose audit period ended more than a year ago. Is that a problem, and what do you do about it? This lesson covers vendor monitoring (vendor registry, vendor assessment, compliance attestation, right to audit, service-level monitoring, penetration testing), the constraints that limit oversight and testing, and rules of engagement. Then a real script checks a made-up vendor registry, and a lab pen test obeys signed rules: the out-of-scope host is refused, and only the in-scope host is scanned with nmap. CompTIA Security+ SY0-801 lesson SP8-R05.

Everything you need is in the video: every command and output is on screen. Pause any time.

Exam objective (SY0-801 v2.0): 5.3 Explain the processes associated with third-party risk assessment and management (vendor monitoring; limitations/constraints; rules of engagement).

Chapters
0:00 The SOC 2 report is a year old
0:28 Vendor monitoring: six tools
1:14 Check the vendor registry
1:49 Now what? Bridge letter, right to audit
2:18 Constraints
3:05 Rules of engagement
3:24 Out of scope: refused
3:37 In scope: the nmap scan
3:50 Exam shortcut
4:16 Your turn: draft rules of engagement
4:40 One good answer
5:00 Next lesson

Lab results (20 Nov 2026, three identical runs). The vendors, dates and rules of engagement are SYNTHETIC; the scope check and the nmap scan are real (lab hosts in network namespaces).
vendor_review.py (as of 2026-11-15, limit 365 days): Brightwage SOC 2 Type II report period ended 380 days ago (STALE REPORT), last assessed 423 days ago (ASSESS DUE); Ledgerline OK; Parcelhub OK; Cloudnest has no right-to-audit clause (NO AUDIT).
scoped_scan.sh: 10.88.5.30 (shared host, out of scope) REFUSED; 10.88.5.20 (in scope) scanned with nmap -sT -Pn -p 1-1024: 22/tcp open ssh, 443/tcp open https; results to both signatories only.

Now what for a stale report: ask for the current report or a bridge letter (the vendor's own statement that nothing important changed since the audit period; it buys time, it does not replace the report); if they can't show it, use the right to audit; record the gap in the risk register with an owner and a date.

Constraints: staffing, resource availability, environment, legal and regulatory factors, geography/jurisdiction, financial/ROI, vendor lock-in, assurance mechanisms.

Practice answer (rules of engagement for a Parcelhub pen test): both sides sign; only the named shipping hosts in scope; shared and customer systems out of scope; a quiet, agreed window; scans and web tests, no denial of service; if anything breaks or real customer data shows up, stop and call.

Exam shortcut: registry = lists vendors; assessment = checks them; attestation = independent proof; right to audit = you inspect them; service-level monitoring = measure the SLA; pen testing = signed rules of engagement (scope, window, methods, contacts); people, money, law, location or lock-in holding you back = constraints.

Course start: https://youtu.be/oCFb7dSY8FI
Next lesson: SP8-R06 Security Compliance and Privacy: Monitoring, Consequences and Data Rights.

Tools: nmap, ip netns, ss, python3 (vendor_review.py), bash (scoped_scan.sh).

Why does interoperability matter for AI agents? Agents need open access to all your data, across any engine, model, or cloud. When your data catalog locks you into one vendor, it limits your AI choices too.
In this video, we compare how Snowflake and Databricks approach interoperability. We cover open table formats like Apache Iceberg, open catalog standards, and what it takes to keep control of your data as AI evolves.

The bottom line: The agentic enterprise needs open data. Choose a platform that keeps your data, engines, and AI models in your control.

metadata.title: Databricks vs Snowflake 2026: Pricing, AI, Security Compared
metadata.author: Kanerika Inc.
metadata.shortDescription:
0:00 Databricks and Snowflake Turf War
1:47 Origins: Data Lakehouse vs Cloud-Native
3:20 ETL Speed vs Instant SQL Performance
3:57 Pricing: Credits vs Dual-Layer DBUs
5:50 Security Models and Data Sharing
7:23 AI Capabilities: MLflow vs Cortex AI
8:49 Kanerika's Snowflake and Databricks Case Studies
11:42 Developer Experience and the Azure Factor

📌 Overview
Choosing between Databricks and Snowflake in 2026 is no longer a simple "warehouse vs. lakehouse" decision — both platforms have crossed $5 billion in revenue and are now building directly into each other's territory. In this episode of The Digital Shift, we break down where each platform actually came from (Apache Spark's data lakehouse vs. Snowflake's proprietary cloud-native architecture), how their pricing models differ (Snowflake's credit-based system vs. Databricks' dual-layer DBU model), and how their security and data-sharing approaches diverge. We also compare their AI capabilities — Databricks' MLflow and native GPU support versus Snowflake's SQL-first Cortex AI — and walk through two real Kanerika client projects that show each platform's strengths in action. If you're an enterprise leader trying to decide which platform fits your team, your budget, and your AI roadmap, this is the comparison you need.

🎯 Key Takeaways
• Databricks was built on Apache Spark's data lakehouse model (storage decoupled from compute, works directly on raw/unstructured data); Snowflake uses a proprietary cloud-native architecture optimized for structured SQL analytics.
• Databricks can process large-scale ETL up to 12x faster on messy, unstructured data, while Snowflake's virtual warehouses resume in fractions of a second for instant business intelligence queries.
• Pricing differs fundamentally: Snowflake's credit-based billing with autosuspend gives predictable costs, while Databricks' dual-layer DBU model requires separate cloud infrastructure billing but allows up to ~40% savings via spot instances.
• Snowflake is "secure by default" with built-in encryption and mandatory MFA plus a 1,000+ app marketplace, while Databricks' Unity Catalog offers flexible, user-configured governance and the open Delta Sharing protocol.
• On AI, Databricks leads with MLflow, Mosaic AI, and native GPU support for custom deep learning, while Snowflake's Cortex AI brings SQL-based predictive AI directly to business analysts.
• In a Kanerika medtech project, migrating to Snowflake + Power BI cut executive reporting time by 61% and lifted data-driven decisions by 25%; in a separate AI sales intelligence project, moving unstructured PDF processing to Databricks delivered 80% faster processing and 95% better metadata accuracy.

Snowflake Technology: https://kanerika.com/technology/snowflake/

💼 About Kanerika
Kanerika is an AI-first data and automation consulting firm founded in 2015, headquartered in Austin, Texas, with 300+ professionals serving 100+ enterprise clients worldwide. As both a Databricks Consulting Partner and a Snowflake Select Tier Partner, Kanerika helps enterprises assess their data architecture, team skills, and AI goals to design the right lakehouse or warehouse strategy — not a one-size-fits-all answer.

📅 Ready to build the right data platform strategy for your enterprise? Book a free consultation: https://kanerika.com/contact-us/

So, even if the recipient doesn't use Databricks? >> Exactly. It works even if the recipient company has never purchased a Databricks license in their life. >> Wow. Deep learning requires processing thousands of complex mathematical calculations simultaneously, which is exactly the mechanism GPUs are built for. Databricks handles that hardware acceleration natively. >> Meanwhile, Snowflake is playing a highly aggressive game of catch-up. >> They really are. They utilize simple SQL functions to call upon pre-trained models. Snowflake is basically attempting to democratize AI by bringing the predictive capabilities directly to the SQL analysts who already understand the business logic. >> Right, the people who actually know what the data means. >> Exactly. metadata.title: Databricks vs Snowflake -Complete Architectural and Technical Decision Framework
metadata.author: The Data & AI Playground
metadata.shortDescription:
Databricks or Snowflake? I break down the real architecture, honest tradeoffs, and a 5-question framework so you can make this decision once — and get it right.
Chapters:
0:00 – Why this decision goes wrong
0:30 – The landscape: how we got here
1:15 – Architecture deep dive (the apartment vs. the house)
3:00 – Technical fit across 6 dimensions
5:15 – Business lens: team, cost model & data maturity
6:45 – 5-question decision framework
7:30 – Wrap up
🔑 What you'll learn:
→ Snowflake's three-layer architecture vs. the Databricks Lakehouse model
→ Which platform wins for SQL analytics, data engineering, ML/AI, and streaming
→ How to think about total cost of ownership (not just the platform bill)
→ When to run both — and why that's a legitimate architecture
📌 Relevant for: data engineers, analytics engineers, data architects, CTOs, and anyone evaluating a modern data stack.

🔔 Subscribe for Data & AI Topics
#Databricks #Snowflake #DataEngineering #Data #ai #machinelearning #dataarchitecture

There are three factors that often determine whether the whole thing succeeds or fails. The first one is team composition, the most underrated factor in this entire decision. Snowflake is like handing someone a really powerful calculator. If your team lives in SQL, analyst, BI developers, analytics engineer, they're productive on day one. Low learning curve, high time to value. Whereas Databricks is more like handing someone a full engineering workbench. Powerful, flexible, capable of incredible things, but you need people who know how to use it. Python, Spark, distributed computing, notebook-driven workflows. If that skill set isn't already on your team, budget seriously for the ramp-up time. The best platform in the world is useless if your team cannot operate it. The next comes cost model, and this one trips people up. Neither platform is inherently cheaper. It depends entirely on your workload pattern. Snowflake bills per seconds of virtual warehouse compute. Bursty, unpredictable workloads with lot of idle time. Auto suspend makes this genuinely efficient. You only pay when the engines are running. Think of it like paying for a taxi. You pay per trip, nothing when you're not riding. Whereas, Databricks uses DBU pricing, which is Databricks units, which varies by workload tier and cluster type. Better for sustained long-running pipelines and email training when it's well tuned. More like leasing a car, better value if you're driving constantly, but the pricing model is more complex and needs active monitoring. But here's the real trap. The total cost of ownership isn't just the platform bill. It's the platform spend plus engineering hours to manage it, plus operational overhead, plus migration cost if you pick the wrong one. Snowflake's simplicity saves ops hours. Databricks flexibility costs upfront platform engineering. Model all three before you decide. Data maturity, where are you actually at? Early stage, SQL heavy team, need time to value fast, which is Snowflake. Mid stage, analytics is covered, now building out ML and real-time use cases. Databricks or a hybrid model would work out. Advanced, running end-to-end AI workflow with large engineering team, Databricks becomes your center of gravity, and plenty of mature organizations run both Databricks as the engineering and ML backbone, Snowflake as a clean, governed analytics layer on top. That's not indecision, that's a proven, real-world architecture. Answer these five questions honestly, and you'll figure out which tool to use. Number one, primary workload. SQL analytics and BI go with Snowflake. Data engineering, ML pipeline streaming, go with Databricks. Number two, primary user. Unless BI developers, go with Snowflake. Data engineers, data scientists, go with Databricks. Number three, ML ambition. Predictive analytics through SQL is enough, Snowflake Cortex covers you fully. Full MLops life cycle, training, serving, monitoring, go with Databricks, no contest. Number four, how much does openness matter? Vendor lock-in is acceptable for operational simplicity, go with Snowflake. Open formats and data portability are your strategic requirement, go with Databricks. Number five, data maturity. Early stage, moving fast, needs simplicity, Snowflake speed to value wins here. Scaling long-term with a technical team, take Databricks seriously. If your answers are mostly Snowflake, go with it. If your answers are mostly Databricks, invest in lakehouse. If it is a split, you are a hybrid candidate and that's completely legitimate architecture. At the end of the day, this was never about which platform is better in some abstract sense, it's about fit to your workloads, your team skill, and where you want to be in the next three years. Get the fit right and the platform choice becomes obvious. Next in Databricks series is a workspace tour, so stay tuned.

metadata.shortDescription:
Full playlist on the subject is at https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLaXPzaU2e3gY Defending against malicious license audits prevents unexpected enterprise costs. Learn to protect your organization from vendor aggression.

This briefing explains how enterprise procurement can shift from a reactive function to a strategic defensive asset. We detail how to identify common vendor tactics like the anchoring effect and artificial deadlines that often lead to unfavorable contract outcomes. By focusing on auditable metrics instead of marketing narratives, your team can maintain control during high-stakes software negotiations.

Understanding these mechanics is essential for IT leaders who want to counter aggressive sales maneuvers. We provide a framework to ensure your infrastructure remains sustainable by evaluating vendor demands objectively. Use these insights to build a more resilient procurement strategy and stop malicious license audits from impacting your bottom line.

Virtualization Options LLC - A Colorado-based Research, Education, and Advisory Organization

Email Contact: virtualizationoptions@protonmail.com
YouTube Sites:
https://www.virtualizationoptions.com
https://www.rfidetectives.com

metadata.title: Why 2024 will be known as 📈 inflection point for marketplaces and partners -  w/ Jay McBain, Canalys
metadata.author: Partner Insight
metadata.shortDescription:
"2024, in the history books, will be known as an 📈 inflection point. 43 years into our broader partner channel… major things are happening" - stressed the magnitude of the shift Jay McBain in our recent How to Unlock Next-Gen Cloud GTM event.

Jay McBain is Chief Analyst, Channels, Partnerships & Ecosystems at Canalys, whose insights on partnerships are unmatched. Jay has been a pioneer in recognizing the shift towards #cloud  #marketplaces as they become essential GTM strategies. 

In his keynote, he outlined the rapid evolution of GTM caused by the new digital-first buyer, rise of marketplaces as ultimate tech platforms, and how this transforms the role of partners.

3 Insights from Jay's keynote:

📊  Marketplaces Orchestrate the 7-Layer Stack
🏆 Hyperscalers Vie for #Platform Dominance
🤝 Partners are Indispensable in a $5 Trillion Market

___
💡 Master marketplaces with Cloud GTM Leader course

Last chance to join us on April 9th for 5-weeks deep dive on accelerating 
#growth in marketplaces of Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud in a community of great alliance leaders.

https://partnerinsight.io/course-marketplaces


📩 Learn more insights like this in my newsletter 
https://partnerinsight.substack.com/

metadata.title: Get the Most Value from Value Added Resellers
metadata.author: Staying Connected
metadata.shortDescription:
Value added resellers are an important part of the ICT ecosystem and without them, a lot of great products and services would never make it to the enterprise.  But what are value added resellers, or VARs, and why do they exist?

 Listen to this 10-minute podcast as Ben Fox, one of TC2’s Managing Directors, and Joe Schmidt describe what VARs do, explain some of the nuances of their pricing, and offer up some tips to help you get the most value from your value added reseller.

 If you would like to learn more about our experience in this space, please visit our  Hardware & Licensing and Success Stories webpages.

metadata.title: Why Most ISVs Get Channel Wrong | Building an Enterprise Software Ecosystem
metadata.author: Luasai
metadata.shortDescription:
Selling enterprise software isn't just a sales problem. It's an ecosystem problem.

In this conversation, Luasai co-founders Luke Hasty and Zaheer Javed unpack what they've learned from working across enterprise software sales, channel, partners and transactions—and why many ISVs approach channel the wrong way.

They discuss why direct sales alone becomes limiting as companies scale, what early-stage ISVs actually need from channel, why recruiting hundreds of partners can backfire, and how the best enterprise sellers use partners as an extension of their own team.

The conversation also covers cloud marketplaces, reseller economics, AI and agentic procurement, the changing role of channel teams, and a practical three-stage model for building an ecosystem as an ISV grows.

Topics include: building channel at Series A and beyond, sales vs. distribution, choosing the right partners, reseller margins and deal control, cloud marketplaces, AI in enterprise software, partner-led pipeline, and making enterprise software easier to buy.

Luke and Zaheer also explain where Luasai fits: using partner and account intelligence to help ISVs identify the right routes to market, activate the right partners and streamline transactions through the enterprise software ecosystem.

Luasai — infrastructure for how enterprise software gets sold, partnered and transacted.
